books.title: I'd Like To Be
books.art_why: Whimsical imagined scenes with dragons, wizards and superheroes cannot be photographed.

pages.text: I’d Like to Be.
pages.brief: A young child stands alone on a plain background, head tipped to one side with a dreaming, hopeful expression, one hand raised as if counting off ideas. The child's face is bright and thoughtful, showing a mind full of possibilities about what to be when grown.

pages.text: I’d like to be a cook and make a dish with meats and sweets and veggies and fish. I’d learn to cook, not by the book but by testing, tasting, and taking a look. I’d Like to Be.
pages.brief: The child stands at a wide table scattered with meats, sweets, vegetables and fish, stirring and tasting from a big bowl. Flour and spoons are within reach. The child leans in close, nose wrinkled in concentration, checking the dish by look and taste rather than by any book.

pages.text: See my kitchen? Come and pitch in! My stew ’s alive with corn and chives.
pages.brief: The child stands proudly beside a big kitchen stove, waving a wooden spoon, with a steaming pot of stew full of corn kernels and green chives bubbling on the burner. Pots and pans hang around the busy kitchen, and the child grins, inviting someone to come in and join the cooking.

pages.text: I’d like to be a maker of video games full of dragons and wizards with crazy names. The game I’d write would feature knights who run and jump and get in fights. I’d Like to Be.
pages.brief: The child sits at a computer designing a video game, and the screen glows with dragons, wizards in pointed hats and armored knights who run, jump and swing swords at one another. The child's hands are on the keyboard, eyes wide with excitement at the wild, funny names and characters.

pages.text: This game is a fun fantasy. I’d like it if you played with me!
pages.brief: The child leans toward a friend beside the glowing game screen, pointing at the fantasy world of dragons and knights playing out on it, one hand held out offering a controller. Both faces are lit by the screen, eager to share the fun of the game.

pages.text: I’d like to gaze into the sky, and take notes on what’s passing by. I’d search for planets near and far. I’d help to name each brand new star. I’d Like to Be.
pages.brief: The child lies back on a grassy hill at night, a notebook and pencil in hand, gazing up at a sky crowded with stars and a planet or two drifting past. The child scribbles notes, searching the sky near and far for something new to name.

pages.text: I would help discover things, from galaxies to Saturn’s rings.
pages.brief: The child kneels over a spread notebook of sketched galaxies and a ringed planet like Saturn, pencil moving quickly, pointing up at the sky and then down at the page. Stars and swirling spiral shapes fill the drawings as the child works out what has been discovered.

pages.text: I’d like to be a vet who helps sick cats, and barking dogs and hurting bats. People would bring their pets to me. I would help them stay healthy. I’d Like to Be.
pages.brief: The child, wearing a vet's coat, kneels in a clinic with a sick cat curled in a basket, a barking dog tugging at a leash and a bat held gently in cupped hands. People stand nearby holding their pets, waiting for help, while the child soothes each animal.

pages.text: I’d heal their cuts and fix their legs, and help with birds who lay bad eggs.
pages.brief: The child vet carefully wraps a bandage on a dog's cut leg and splints a small bird's injured wing, with the cat and bat watching from a nearby table. A nest with a cracked, bad egg sits close by, and the child leans over it with gentle, careful hands.

pages.text: I’d like to be an artist for comic books. I’d draw superheroes and pirate’s hooks and evil people who’d destroy man or woman, girl or boy. I’d Like to Be.
pages.brief: The child sits at a drawing desk covered with comic pages, inking a bold superhero with a cape, a pirate's curved hook and scowling villains with clenched fists. Pens and brushes are scattered about, and the child bends low over the paper, deep in the story.

pages.text: Their plots won’t make it off the ground— not with Super Boy around.
pages.brief: The child's comic page comes alive: a small caped hero leaps through the panel, fists out, while the villains tumble backward, their plans collapsing around them. The child grins, one hand raised, as the heroic character wins the day.

pages.text: I’d like to fix cool cars in an auto shop. I’d get them going when they stop. I’d do repairs and make them run. That is my idea of fun. I’d Like to Be.
pages.brief: The child stands in an auto shop beside a cool car with its hood propped open, wrench in hand, tools laid out on a bench and tires stacked in the corner. The child looks happy and ready to do repairs and get the car running again.

pages.text: I’d fix their engines when they stall. Getting greasy is a ball!
pages.brief: The child leans over a stalled engine, sleeves rolled up, hands black with grease, tightening a bolt with a wrench while grinning broadly. Smudges of oil mark the child's cheek, and the shop around is busy with parts and tools.

pages.text: Life has endless possibilities. What in the world would you like to be? I’d Like to Be.
pages.brief: The child stands facing the reader with arms spread wide and a big smile, surrounded by small hints of every job imagined before. The child looks curious and inviting, asking the reader to think about what they would like to be.

books.title: Summer Olympic Events
books.art_why: The Summer Olympics and its athletes exist in the real world today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: Summer Olympic Events.
pages.brief: A bright summer scene at an Olympic stadium, with athletes in sportswear standing together on a track and a field. The sun shines over the stadium, and people are ready for different Summer Olympic events to begin.

pages.text: Summer Olympics Host Cities Athens, Greece 2004 Montreal, Canada 1976 Beijing, China 2008 Moscow, Russia 1980 London, England 2012 Los Angeles, California 1984 Rio de Janeiro, Brazil 2016 Seoul, South Korea 1988 Tokyo, Japan 2021* Barcelona, Spain 1992 Paris, France 2024 Atlanta, Georgia 1996 Sydney, Australia 2000 Los Angeles, California 2028 The Summer Olympic Games The Summer Olympics are held every four years. They are held in different cities around the world.
pages.brief: A large globe shows many different cities across the world, with groups of athletes standing in different countries. The scene shows that the Summer Olympic Games are held in different cities around the world every four years.

pages.text: Athletes at the Games compete to win medals for their countries. They participate in hundreds of events. Let’s look at some events.
pages.brief: Athletes from many countries stand together in a large Olympic stadium, each wearing sportswear. One athlete holds up a shining medal, while others smile and prepare to compete in hundreds of different events. A crowd watches from the stands under a bright sky.

pages.text: Water Sports One water sport is swimming. Some swimming races are short, and swimmers swim only two lengths of the pool. Other races are longer.
pages.brief: Swimmers race in a long swimming pool, with water splashing around them. Some swimmers swim only two lengths of the pool in short races, while other swimmers swim much longer races. They stretch their arms and kick as they move through the water.

pages.text: Some swimming races use only one kind of stroke. In one race, swimmers can choose the type of stroke they want to use.
pages.brief: Several swimmers move through a pool in a race. In one race, the swimmers use only one kind of stroke. In another race beside them, swimmers choose the type of stroke they want to use as they race through the water.

pages.text: Diving is another water sport. In diving events, divers jump from high above the water, and they twist, flip and turn while in the air. They get points for how well they dive.
pages.brief: A diver stands high above a swimming pool, then jumps into the air. The diver twists, flips, and turns above the water during the dive. The diver earns points for how well the dive is done, and the pool shines below.

pages.text: Track and Field Track and field events include running, throwing, and jumping competitions. The marathon is the longest running event, and the shortest races are called dashes.
pages.brief: Athletes take part in track and field events on a stadium field. A marathon runner runs a long distance, while dash runners sprint on a short track. Nearby, other athletes prepare to throw objects and jump in their competitions.

pages.text: In throwing events, athletes throw objects as far as they can. People competing in these events must be very strong.
pages.brief: Strong athletes stand in a throwing area and throw objects as far as they can. One athlete winds up and releases an object across the field, while other athletes watch and prepare for their turn. Their muscles strain with effort under a bright sky.

pages.text: In jumping events, athletes jump high or far. In the high jump, athletes leap over a bar. The bar is raised higher and higher until only one person can jump it. In the long jump, athletes leap as far as they can.
pages.brief: Athletes compete in jumping events. A high jumper leaps over a bar that is raised higher and higher, until only one person can clear it. Nearby, a long jumper runs and leaps as far as possible into a sandy landing area.

pages.text: Gymnastics Gymnasts leap, flip, and twirl through the air. They need strength, skill, and perfect timing.
pages.brief: Two gymnasts leap, flip, and twirl through the air in a bright gymnastics hall. One gymnast arches through a graceful flip while another lands on a mat, showing strength, skill, and perfect timing. Their bodies move with control and speed.

pages.text: One event is the balance beam. Gymnasts must balance on the beam while they turn and flip.
pages.brief: A gymnast balances on a narrow balance beam in a gymnastics hall. She turns and flips while keeping her body steady on the beam, with her arms out for balance. Her movement needs careful control and timing.

pages.text: Another event is the rings. Gymnasts hold onto the rings and flip their bodies in circles.
pages.brief: A gymnast holds onto two hanging rings and flips his body in circles through the air. His arms are strong as he supports his weight above the floor. The rings hang from above in a bright gymnastics hall.

pages.text: Event Categories The Summer Olympics include many sports with hundreds of events. Which events do you like? Summer Olympic Sports.
pages.brief: Many Summer Olympic athletes gather together in a bright stadium, showing different sports from the Games. Swimmers, runners, divers, gymnasts, and throwers stand side by side. The wide scene shows many different sports and hundreds of events for viewers to enjoy.

books.title: Ships and Boats
books.art_why: Ships and boats are real objects that exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction Ships and boats are part of our history. Before cars, trains, or airplanes, they were the fastest way to travel. Even today, they continue to get bigger and faster.
pages.brief: A large ship and a smaller boat on the water, with a car, a train, and an airplane shown in the background. The scene illustrates that ships and boats were the fastest way to travel before those vehicles and continue to get bigger and faster.

pages.text: Early Ships and Boats The first boats were dugout canoes. They were made from just one log. They were used in rivers, lakes, and oceans around the world. People used poles to push some of these boats.
pages.brief: A dugout canoe made from a single log floats on a river, with two people standing inside using long poles to push it through the water. The canoe is shown on a calm river with trees along the bank.

pages.text: Other boats used paddles or oars. These are long pieces of wood with wide, flat ends. They pushed against the water to move the boat ahead. Later, people made boats with wooden frames. They covered the frames with bark, reeds, or animal skins.
pages.brief: A person in a small boat uses a long wooden paddle with a wide, flat end to push against the water. Next to it, a boat made of a wooden frame covered with animal skin floats on the water.

pages.text: Some people built boats that could sail well beyond the islands where they lived. They took two canoes and joined them with large wooden poles. This kind of boat was called a catamaran. These boats could travel very fast. They also allowed safe travel from one island to another.
pages.brief: A catamaran made of two canoes joined by large wooden poles sails on the ocean away from a small island. People on board calmly steer the fast boat safely toward another island in the distance.

pages.text: Some frame ships were much larger than log boats. Many people could row at the same time. These ships were called galleys. At times they carried hundreds of rowers.
pages.brief: A large galley ship with a wooden frame, much bigger than a log boat, sits on the sea. Many rowers sit in rows along the sides, pulling long oars together to move the ship forward.

pages.text: Sails made from strong cloth were also used to move boats. The sails caught the wind. The wind pushed the boat. As ships became bigger, they needed more sails. Sailing ships carried explorers all around the world.
pages.brief: A large sailing ship with many strong cloth sails catching the wind on the open ocean. Explorers stand on deck as the ship steadily travels around the world, with the strong wind pushing it forward.

pages.text: Modern Ships and Boats Today, many boats are made of metal and plastic. Many ships and boats use electricity to turn propellers. The propellers push the boat through the water. Boats with propellers are everywhere.
pages.brief: A modern boat made of metal and plastic on the water, with a propeller spinning under the surface. The propeller is turned by electricity and pushes the boat forward, and similar boats are visible in the background.

pages.text: Cruise ships are like floating hotels. They can carry thousands of people. Huge tankers carry oil and gas over the ocean.
pages.brief: A huge cruise ship that looks like a floating hotel, with thousands of people on its decks, sailing steadily on the ocean. Nearby, a very massive tanker carries oil and gas across the calm water.

pages.text: Tugboats push and pull larger ships. Ferryboats carry cars and people. Fireboats put out fires on other ships.
pages.brief: A small tugboat pushing a much larger ship in a busy harbor. A ferryboat loaded with several cars and people calmly crosses the water, while a large fireboat sprays water onto a burning ship nearby.

pages.text: Many countries use ships and boats, large and small, to defend their coasts. Submarines move under the water. Planes and helicopters take off and land on aircraft carriers.
pages.brief: A large aircraft carrier at sea with many planes and helicopters taking off and landing on its deck. A submarine slowly moves under the deep water nearby, and several smaller boats quickly defend the coast.

pages.text: People still use smaller boats for fishing, fun, and sport. Many of these boats still use paddles or oars.
pages.brief: People in small boats on a quiet lake, using paddles and oars for fishing, fun, and sport. One person fishes from a small boat while another rows with oars, and a third paddles for sport.

pages.text: Conclusion Ships and boats have changed a lot over the years. Even so, they are still an important way to move quickly over the water.
pages.brief: A modern fast boat and an older sailing ship on the water together, showing how ships and boats have changed over the years. The fast boat speeds across the water, still an important way to move quickly.

books.title: Where's the Joey?
books.art_why: Real marsupials and habitats exist today.

pages.text: What’s a Joey? A joey is a baby marsupial (mar-SOO-pee-ul). A marsupial is an unusual type of animal. Its babies are carried in a pouch, or pocket, on the mother’s belly. As it grows, the little joey stays hidden inside the pouch.
pages.brief: A mother marsupial stands with a tiny baby joey tucked inside the pouch on her belly. The joey is hidden in the pouch, small and safe, while the mother carries it. The joey stays inside as it grows.

pages.text: Safe inside, the tiny joey drinks milk and grows while it is carried around. Even after it can walk, the joey may still ride in mom’s pouch. Where’s the Joey?
pages.brief: Inside the mother’s pouch, the tiny joey drinks milk and grows while she carries it around. Later, even after the joey can walk, it may still ride in mom’s pouch. The joey is safe inside there.

pages.text: There are over three hundred types of marsupials. Most of them live in Australia (aw-STRAYL-yuh) and eat plants. Let’s look at a few kinds of marsupials and their joeys.
pages.brief: Many different marsupials stand together in Australia, most of them eating plants. A few kinds of marsupials have their joeys nearby. There are over three hundred types of marsupials in the world. Most live in Australia.

pages.text: A Jumping Joey This joey stays in its mother’s pouch for eight months while it grows very tall. Its feet and tail grow very long, too. Can you guess what it is? Where’s the Joey?
pages.brief: A jumping joey stays inside its mother’s pouch for eight months while it grows very tall. Its feet and tail grow very long, too. The mother carries the joey as it grows. The joey is hidden in the pouch.

pages.text: It’s a red kangaroo! A red kangaroo is the largest marsupial. It can stand over six feet tall and weigh 200 lbs (91 kg). It can jump 30 feet (9 m) with each leap!
pages.brief: A red kangaroo, the largest marsupial, stands tall and strong. It can stand over six feet tall and weigh 200 lbs. With its long feet and tail, it leaps 30 feet through the air. It is a big jumper.

pages.text: A Joey That Lives in a Tree When grown, this little joey will look like a furry teddy bear with big ears. It will live most of its life sitting in trees and eating leaves. Can you guess what it is? Where’s the Joey?
pages.brief: A little joey with big ears sits in a tree, eating leaves. When grown, it will look like a furry teddy bear. It will spend most of its life sitting in trees and eating leaves.

pages.text: It’s a koala! A koala lives, eats, and sleeps in eucalyptus (yoo-kuh-LIP-tus) trees. It is happy just to sit and eat lots of leaves every day. A koala usually only walks around at night.
pages.brief: A koala sits in a eucalyptus tree, eating lots of leaves. It lives, eats, and sleeps in these trees. The koala usually walks around only at night. It is happy to sit and eat leaves every day.

pages.text: Joey the Screamer This marsupial mom might carry three or four noisy joeys in her pouch at one time. Her little joeys can scream very loudly. What are they? Where’s the Joey?
pages.brief: A marsupial mother carries three or four noisy joeys in her pouch at one time. The little joeys have their mouths open and scream very loudly. The mother stands with all of them tucked in her pouch.

pages.text: They are Tasmanian devils! The Tasmanian devil gets its name from its loud screams, sharp teeth, bad smell, and wild look. It is a meat-eater, and lives only on the island of Tasmania (taz-MAY-nee-uh).
pages.brief: A Tasmanian devil shows sharp teeth and a wild look. It has loud screams and lives only on the island of Tasmania. This meat-eater is named for its screams, sharp teeth, bad smell, and wild look.

pages.text: Do You Know? All marsupial pouches are not the same. A kangaroo’s pouch opens sideways across the front of its mother. Digging marsupials, such as wombats, koalas, and Tasmanian devils, all have pouches that open towards the rear of the mother. The rear-facing pouch protects the baby from flying dirt or tree bark when the mother is digging. Where’s the Joey?
pages.brief: A kangaroo mother has a pouch that opens sideways across the front of her body. A wombat digs, and its rear-facing pouch protects the baby inside from flying dirt. Koalas and Tasmanian devils also have rear-facing pouches.

pages.text: Protecting the Marsupials Most marsupials eat plants, and many, like the koala, live quietly in forests. When those forests are cut down, their homes, food, and safety are lost. Other marsupials have lost their sources of food to herds of grazing cows or growing cities.
pages.brief: A koala sits quietly in a forest, but the trees around it have been cut down. Cows graze nearby, and city buildings grow in the distance. The marsupials lose their homes, food, and safety when forests are cut down.

pages.text: Marsupials Are Special Animals Most marsupials and their joeys live in only one place on Earth. We need to protect their special habitats and food sources—so we will always know where the joeys are. Learn More About Marsupials Australian marsupials look different from most animals— and they have unusual names, too. Where’s the Joey?
pages.brief: A mother marsupial with a joey in her pouch stands in an Australian habitat. Around her are other Australian marsupials with joeys, in special places with food sources. Most live in only one place on Earth. Their special habitats and food sources need protection.

books.title: Día de los Muertos
books.art_why: The holiday, parades, families, altars and art can all be photographed today.

pages.text: Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead)
pages.brief: A warm, festive Día de los Muertos scene with people of different ages gathered together in a bright, welcoming space. They smile and share the holiday’s joyful mood, introducing a celebration that honors loved ones.

pages.text: When and Where? People all over the world celebrate Día de los Muertos, or “Day of the Dead.” People in Mexico have celebrated holidays like this one for thousands of years. All over the United States, people hold parades and celebrations. These usually take place around November 1 and 2.
pages.brief: In Mexico, families celebrate with parades and joyful gatherings, while in cities across the United States people also hold parades and celebrations. The festive scenes suggest early November, with people of all ages taking part outdoors.

pages.text: Is It Halloween? Día de los Muertos might seem like Halloween. The two holidays are different, though. Halloween is often about scaring people. Día de los Muertos is a time of joy. People remember and celebrate loved ones who have died.
pages.brief: A split scene shows children in spooky Halloween costumes on one side, looking playful and scary. On the other side, a family smiles together in a warm, joyful remembrance of loved ones who have died, showing the difference between the two holidays.

pages.text: Lidia’s Día de los Muertos Lidia Terán-Cooper grew up in Mexico. Lidia and her family spent every Día de los Muertos at the cemetery. The family brought flowers and a picnic.
pages.brief: Young Lidia Terán-Cooper stands with her family at a cemetery in Mexico. They carry flowers and set out a picnic among the graves, spending Día de los Muertos together in warm daylight. They look calm and close.

pages.text: They told stories about those who had died. Bands played special songs. Lidia and the other children danced and played all day. Día de los Muertos was always a happy day for Lidia.
pages.brief: At the cemetery, a band plays special songs while Lidia and other children dance and play. Adults tell stories about loved ones who died, and everyone smiles during this happy Día de los Muertos day.

pages.text: Lidia lives in the United States now. Lidia and her family walk in the parade in Tucson (TOO-sawn), Arizona, every year.
pages.brief: Lidia Terán-Cooper now lives in the United States. She and her family walk together in a colorful parade in Tucson, Arizona, smiling among other participants as they celebrate Día de los Muertos. The street is bright and busy.

pages.text: Before the parade, Lidia makes masks. Children and adults paint the masks and wear them in the parade.
pages.brief: Before the parade, Lidia makes masks at a table in a busy room. Children and adults paint the masks with bright colors, then wear them, preparing together for the parade. Everyone looks focused and cheerful.

pages.text: Day of the Dead for Children Some places have a parade for children. Children decorate cardboard wings to wear. They paint their faces and put on costumes.
pages.brief: Children get ready for a children’s parade. They decorate cardboard wings to wear, paint their faces, and put on costumes, standing together in a cheerful group before the celebration. They smile while they work together.

pages.text: Altars Día de los Muertos has many other traditions. Some people build altars in their homes. The altars are covered with cloth. The family puts up photos of the person who has died. They might add a favorite item or piece of clothing of the loved one.
pages.brief: In a home, a family builds an altar covered with cloth. They place photos of the person who died and add a favorite item or piece of clothing, arranging the altar carefully together. They look thoughtful.

pages.text: The family lights candles around the altars. They also make special bread. They might even leave a favorite drink. Flowers, skeleton toys, and dolls also decorate the altars.
pages.brief: Around the home altar, the family lights candles. They make special bread and leave a favorite drink, then decorate with flowers, skeleton toys, and dolls. The altar glows warmly with many offerings. Everyone gathers nearby.

pages.text: Sugar Skulls Some people make sugar skulls. People decorate the sugar skulls with colorful frosting. Children love eating the sweet skulls.
pages.brief: People make sugar skulls and decorate them with colorful frosting. Children gather around, smiling and eager to eat the sweet skulls, while the bright decorations dry on a table. The scene is cheerful and busy.

pages.text: Art Some artists make paintings for the holiday. The paintings show skeletons dancing and playing music. The art is a way to celebrate friends and family members who have died.
pages.brief: An artist paints a holiday picture in a studio. The painting shows skeletons dancing and playing music, a colorful way to celebrate friends and family members who have died. The artist works with steady care.

pages.text: Full of Life Día de los Muertos helps people to feel better after losing someone they love. Marching in a parade or decorating altars can help them celebrate that special person. No other holiday is so full of life, costumes, masks, joy, memories, and love.
pages.brief: A joyful closing scene shows people marching in a parade in costumes and masks while others decorate an altar. They celebrate a special person with memories, joy, and love, full of life together. Everyone looks happy.

books.title: Tarantula!
books.art_why: Tarantulas are real animals living today, so real photographs are possible.

pages.text: Tarantula!
pages.brief: A single tarantula fills the frame, huge and hairy, standing on dark forest ground or a rock, its eight legs spread and fangs visible, photographed close up so its size and hairiness are dramatic.

pages.text: Introduction What’s huge and hairy, and has fangs that can kill? It’s the biggest spider in the world—the tarantula! Do You Know? There are at least eight hundred different kinds of tarantulas. The biggest kind can grow up to 12 inches (30 cm) long!
pages.brief: A very large tarantula rests on bark or soil, shown in close-up to reveal its thick hairy legs, large body and fangs, giving a clear look at the biggest spider in the world.

pages.text: Where Tarantulas Live Tarantulas live in warm places around the world. Many live in forests, and others live in deserts. More than fifty kinds of tarantulas live in the United States. Some tarantulas live in holes in the ground. Others live under logs or in trees. Do You Know? Some tarantulas are black or brown, but many others are colorful. They may be red, orange, yellow, pink, blue, purple, or other colors. Some have colorful stripes or other markings on their legs or bodies.
pages.brief: Two tarantulas in different settings: one walking across leaf litter in a warm forest, another at the mouth of a desert burrow. A colorful red or orange tarantula shows bright markings on its legs.

pages.text: Hard, Hairy Bodies Like insects and other spiders, tarantulas have a hard covering on their body. As they grow, the covering gets too tight and splits down the middle. After a tarantula pushes out of the old skin, its new skin gets hard.
pages.brief: A tarantula beside its shed skin, the old covering split down the middle on the ground. The spider itself looks fresh and new, its hard outer body smooth and slightly shiny in close-up.

pages.text: A tarantula is covered with hairs. The hairs sense heat, cold, and things that move. Other hairs near its mouth help a tarantula taste and smell. Stiff hairs with points grow on its stomach and back. A tarantula can sting enemies with these hairs.
pages.brief: Extreme close-up of a tarantula's hairy body and back, individual hairs standing out. The spider is still, showing the stiff pointed hairs that cover its stomach and back.

pages.text: The legs of a tarantula have little claws with hairs. The hairs help the tarantula hold on when it climbs. Two little arms near its mouth have sharp parts. The tarantula holds and cuts food with them. Do You Know? Tarantulas have eight eyes—two big ones and six small ones. Even with eight eyes, they cannot see very well. They only see light, dark, and movement.
pages.brief: Close view of a tarantula's leg tip gripping a rough branch, tiny claws and hairs visible, and its small arms and fangs near its mouth as it holds a piece of food.

pages.text: Do You Know? Tarantulas do not weave webs, but they make silk. Tarantulas that live in holes underground cover the walls with silk. Tarantulas that live in trees use silk to make “tents” or tunnels.
pages.brief: Inside a silk-lined underground burrow, walls covered in pale silk, a tarantula sits at rest. Nearby, silk tunnels and tent-like sheets are stretched among tree leaves.

pages.text: Eating and Being Eaten Tarantulas rest during the day and come out at night to hunt. They eat insects, frogs, lizards, bats, mice, and small snakes. They also eat spiders—even other tarantulas.
pages.brief: A tarantula out at night on the forest floor, lit dimly, close to small prey such as an insect and a frog. The spider is alert and moving, its legs spread on the ground.

pages.text: To catch prey, a tarantula sits very still and waits. When an animal comes near, the tarantula jumps and jabs its fangs into it. Venom shoots into the animal and makes it stop moving.
pages.brief: A tarantula lunges at a small animal on the ground, fangs jabbed into it, front legs raised. The scene is captured in the moment of the strike, low on the forest floor.

pages.text: The tarantula drags the animal back home. It uses its jaws and little arms to cut up the animal. It spits juices onto the pieces, which turn to mush. Then the tarantula sucks up a tasty meal. Do You Know? Tarantula fangs can measure up to one-half inch (more than 1 cm) long. Tarantula venom is not usually deadly to humans, but a tarantula bite can hurt a lot and get infected. If you are allergic to the venom, it can be deadly.
pages.brief: A tarantula holds a dead animal under its body, jaws and small arms cutting it, spit turning the pieces to mush on the ground beside its burrow. A clear close view of its fangs.

pages.text: You might think tarantulas are too big to be hunted. Not true! The tarantula hawk—a big wasp—hunts tarantulas as food for its young. A female wasp stings a tarantula, which then stops moving. The wasp lays one egg on the tarantula’s body. When the young insect comes out, it feeds on the tarantula.
pages.brief: A large tarantula hawk wasp with dark wings stands over a still tarantula on the ground, stinging it, with the wasp's body close to the spider. Open dry ground around them.

pages.text: How Safe Are Tarantulas? Many people are scared of tarantulas because they are so big. Tarantulas are harmless if you leave them alone. Some tarantulas are slow and calm. Others are fast and looking for a fight, so don’t mess with them! Do You Know? Many people keep tarantulas as pets. Certain kinds are safe if you learn how to handle them.
pages.brief: A tarantula walking calmly across a person's open hand, gentle and slow, with a blurred natural background. The spider's size is clear against the palm.

pages.text: Do You Know? An adult tarantula can live up to thirty years. Females live much longer than males. People are a bigger danger to tarantulas than any other threat. These amazing spiders are important to the balance of nature. They deserve to be protected.
pages.brief: A large adult female tarantula standing on forest soil, long-legged and hairy, seen in clear daylight. Leaf litter and roots around her show her place in the natural world.

books.title: Strange Plants
books.art_why: All these strange plants exist in the real world today and can be photographed.

pages.text: When we think about plants, we often think of trees, flowers, and grass. Like most plants, these plants have green leaves. They also have roots growing into the ground.
pages.brief: A familiar green scene: a tall tree with leafy branches, a flowering plant and a patch of grass, with roots shown reaching down into the brown ground beneath them. Bright natural daylight in a garden or park, showing the ordinary plants most people picture.

pages.text: Some plants are not like most plants. This book is about some of these strange plants.
pages.brief: A close view of an unusual-looking plant standing apart from ordinary greenery, hinting at the odd plants to come. Soft natural light on its strange leaves and shape, with plain soil or foliage behind it so the plant itself is the focus.

pages.text: Plants called air plants live in trees high above the ground. Their roots are not buried in dirt. Instead, they grow on tree branches. They take moisture from the air, not from the soil as most plants do.
pages.brief: Air plants perched on the branches of a tall tree high above the ground, their roots clinging to bark instead of soil. Sunlight filters through the leaves around them, and the open air surrounds the plants where they take in moisture.

pages.text: Can you imagine plants that eat meat? Well, there are such plants. They eat insects, spiders, and even some other small animals. One well-known meat-eating plant is the Venus flytrap.
pages.brief: A Venus flytrap plant with open trap leaves, one small insect or spider resting inside a leaf. The scene is close up on the plant in damp green surroundings, showing the meat-eating plant ready to catch its small prey.

pages.text: Its leaves look like traps. They have small spikes along their edges. When a critter walks inside a leaf, the leaf snaps shut. The critter is trapped.
pages.brief: Extreme close-up of a Venus flytrap leaf shaped like a trap, with small spikes along its edges. A tiny critter stands inside the leaf, and the leaf is shown snapping shut around it, trapping the small animal inside.

pages.text: The sundew is also a meat-eating plant. It has many sticky hairs on its surface. Insects landing on it get stuck. Then the plant digests the insects. The giant sundew plant of Australia even eats small frogs!
pages.brief: A sundew plant covered in sticky hairs that glisten on its surface, with an insect stuck to one of the hairs. The close view shows the plant's damp, sticky leaves in a natural green setting where insects land.

pages.text: Some plants steal food from other plants. The dodder plant sends rootlike parts into another plant. It sucks food and water from the plant. It is a parasite. A parasite lives off another living thing.
pages.brief: A dodder plant with thin threadlike stems wrapped around another plant, its rootlike parts pushed into the host. The two plants are shown close together in daylight, the dodder drawing food and water from the plant it clings to.

pages.text: Many flowers have bad smells that attract insects. The stapelia flower smells like rotting meat. Flies like the smell, so they fly into the flower. Special powder gets on their bodies. They take the powder to other flowers. The flowers use the powder to make seeds and grow new plants.
pages.brief: A stapelia flower open in the sun, its patterned petals giving off a rotting smell, with flies landing on it. Powder is visible on the flies' bodies as they move about the flower in a dry natural setting.

pages.text: Some plants look like stones. The plants in this picture are called “stone plants” or “living stones.” They live in very hot, dry places. They hold water very well. Their shape helps to hide them so that animals do not eat them.
pages.brief: Stone plants sitting low in very hot, dry ground, their rounded shapes looking just like small stones. Harsh sunlight falls on the dry earth around them, and the plants blend in so animals would pass them by.

pages.text: Some cactus plants are covered with wool-like hairs. The “wool” protects them from daytime heat. It protects them from nighttime cold. The “wool” also helps the cactus plants hold moisture.
pages.brief: A cactus covered in wool-like white hairs, standing in a hot, dry landscape. Bright daytime sun beats down on it, showing the fuzzy coating that shields the cactus from heat, cold and moisture loss.

pages.text: Some trees and shrubs grow out of solid rock. They grow up high where the wind blows strong. Their roots reach down into small cracks for moisture. As the roots grow, they split the rock.
pages.brief: A tree or shrub growing straight out of solid rock high on a windy slope, its roots reaching down into small cracks. The wind blows around the plant as the roots push into the stone and split it apart.

pages.text: Some plants have animals living inside them. Ant colonies live inside ant plants. They use spaces in the plant’s stem as houses. Some spaces are used for raising young ants. Other spaces are used for garbage. The ant plant uses some of this garbage for food.
pages.brief: An ant plant with ants moving over its stem, entering the hollow spaces inside it. Some ants carry young, others haul scraps of garbage into other spaces, all on the plant in a warm, humid natural setting.

pages.text: There are many more kinds of strange plants. Bamboo makes noise when it grows. Some Australian orchids grow and flower completely underground. There are many amazing plants in the world.
pages.brief: A gathering of remarkable plants: bamboo stalks, and an Australian orchid flowering entirely underground in the soil. The scene shows the variety of amazing plants, with bamboo standing tall beside the buried orchid in earthy surroundings.

books.title: Slow and Slower
books.art_why: The book is about real animals that can be photographed.

pages.text: Snail The animal world has some very slow animals in it. One of the very slowest is the snail. Even the fastest snails are pretty slow. In 1995, Archie the snail took two minutes and twenty seconds to crawl 13 inches (33 cm).
pages.brief: A single snail named Archie crawls slowly along the ground, leaving a shiny trail behind it. Its shell and soft body are clearly visible in a simple outdoor setting. The picture shows the snail moving only a short distance, emphasizing its very slow pace.

pages.text: Starfish Snails aren’t the only slow animals. Starfish don’t seem to move at all. At top speed, they just creep along. A starfish needs four minutes to move the length of a man’s arm.
pages.brief: A starfish rests on the seabed among rocks and sand, its arms spread out. It creeps along so slowly that it barely seems to move. The scene shows the starfish in shallow ocean water, with no people or other animals.

pages.text: Three-toed Sloth The three-toed sloth hangs around in trees most of the time. Because it seldom moves, little plants often grow on its fur. A sloth needs about three minutes to crawl the length of two cars.
pages.brief: A three-toed sloth hangs upside down in a tree, gripping a branch with its long claws. Small green plants grow on its shaggy fur. The sloth is shown in the forest canopy, moving very slowly or hardly moving at all.

pages.text: Galapagos Tortoise Humans can walk about eighteen times faster than this giant tortoise. The Galapagos tortoise isn’t fast but it does live a long time. A tortoise can live 150 years or more.
pages.brief: A giant Galapagos tortoise walks slowly across dry, rocky ground. Its large domed shell and thick legs are visible. The tortoise is shown in a natural outdoor setting, moving at a very slow pace, with no people nearby.

pages.text: Gila Monster The desert gila (HEE-luh) monster is about as slow as the Galapagos tortoise. It tries to avoid humans and other animals. If scared, it will hiss loudly then bite quickly.
pages.brief: A gila monster, a patterned desert lizard, stands on sandy ground. It is shown alone, keeping away from people and other animals. Its mouth is open as if it is hissing loudly, ready to bite quickly if scared.

pages.text: How Long Would It Take Each Animal to Travel the Length of a School Bus? Woodcock 6 seconds Slow Loris 25 seconds Tortoise 3 minutes Gila Monster 3 minutes, 15 seconds Swallowtail butterfly 8 seconds Three-toed Sloth 3 minutes, 15 seconds Snail 45 minutes.
pages.brief: A school bus is shown as a long measuring guide, with a woodcock, slow loris, tortoise, gila monster, swallowtail butterfly, three-toed sloth and snail nearby. Each animal is shown as if traveling the length of the bus.

pages.text: Seahorses are found in shallow, warm areas of the ocean that have lots of plants. Seahorse The boney little seahorse has four small fins but it can’t swim fast. It can’t escape an enemy—so it hides. It wraps its tail around a branch to look like it’s a part of the plant.
pages.brief: A small seahorse floats among shallow, warm ocean plants. Its bony body and four small fins are visible. It wraps its tail around a plant branch, hiding among the leaves so it looks like part of the plant.

pages.text: Swallowtail Butterfly The large swallowtail butterfly flaps its big wings very slowly. It flaps, glides, then flaps again. It only flaps its wings about 300 times a minute. A swallowtail flies about twice as fast as a six-year-old child can walk.
pages.brief: A large swallowtail butterfly flies through the air, flapping its big wings slowly. It is shown flapping, then gliding, then flapping again. The butterfly is in a garden or meadow setting, with no people or other animals around.

pages.text: Greenland Shark We think of sharks as fast hunters. However, the Greenland shark is the slowest fish in the ocean. It lives in very cold water so it must use its energy to stay warm.
pages.brief: A Greenland shark swims in very cold, dark ocean water. Its slow body is shown moving through the sea, using energy to stay warm. The shark is alone in the cold water, not hunting fast like other sharks.

pages.text: Slow Loris The loris is a careful little animal with big eyes. It sneaks up on its food at night. The sneaky loris moves so slowly through tree branches that it doesn’t make a sound.
pages.brief: A slow loris with big eyes moves carefully through tree branches at night. It sneaks toward its food, placing its hands and feet slowly so it makes no sound. The small animal is shown among leaves in the dark.

pages.text: Manatee Manatees are large, gentle ocean mammals that just float around. Sometimes they are called “sea cows.” They like to take their time and munch on sea grass. In an hour of munching and floating, a manatee can go about three miles.
pages.brief: A large, gentle manatee floats in the ocean and munches on sea grass. Its big body drifts slowly as it takes its time eating. The scene shows the manatee underwater in a calm, plant-rich area, with no people nearby.

pages.text: Conclusion Some of these animals can speed up when they need to. Some of them are just trying to save their energy. Sometimes they need that energy to heat their bodies. Sometimes what they eat doesn’t give them much energy to begin with. It’s true that slow animals don’t win many races. Still, they have found a way to live that works for them.
pages.brief: Several slow animals are shown together in a calm nature scene. They are shown in a way that suggests their slow lives work for them: some may speed up, some save energy, and some have little energy from food. They do not win races.

books.title: Fast and Faster
books.art_why: Cheetahs, turtles, sailfish, dragonflies and falcons are real animals that can be photographed today.

pages.text: How Fast? How fast can you run? How fast can you swim? Humans are slow compared to some animals. Which animals are the fastest?
pages.brief: A child in shorts and trainers sprints along an outdoor running track, arms pumping. Beside the track another child swims freestyle in a blue pool lane, water splashing. Both move at human speed, slower than many animals.

pages.text: Running The fastest runner is the cheetah. It can go as fast as a car on a highway! Cheetahs can only run that speed for a short time, though. They sprint to catch prey.
pages.brief: A cheetah sprints across dry grassland, long body stretched, legs extended mid-stride, tail trailing. Nearby on a highway a car speeds along the road. The cheetah's burst of speed lasts only a short time as it chases prey.

pages.text: Cheetahs eat gazelles, which are not quite as fast as cheetahs. Gazelles can run fast for a longer time, though.
pages.brief: A cheetah races after a gazelle across open savanna grass, the gazelle leaping ahead. The gazelle keeps running fast for a longer time while the cheetah's sprint fades. Dust rises behind them.

pages.text: Small animals are slower than big animals, but some go fast for their size. The tiger beetle runs 170 times the length of its body in one second. If humans could do that, they could race jet planes!
pages.brief: A close-up photo of a tiger beetle racing over sandy ground, thin legs blurred with speed, its shiny shell catching sunlight. Small as it is, the beetle covers 170 times its own body length in one second.

pages.text: Swimming Turtles are slow on land, yet the world’s fastest reptile is a turtle! It can swim four times as fast as a human.
pages.brief: A turtle swims through clear blue water, front flippers stroking strongly, shell streamlined. On land the same turtle would be slow, yet in water it moves four times as fast as a human.

pages.text: The fastest animal in the sea is the sailfish. In a race, it can easily beat most motorboats. Its cousin the swordfish is almost as fast.
pages.brief: A sailfish speeds through the open sea, tall sail-like fin raised, long bill forward, water spraying. In the distance a motorboat crosses the surface. The sailfish's cousin, the swordfish, is almost as fast.

pages.text: Flying Flying is the fastest way to get around. Some of the fastest animals are birds, bats, and insects. Dragonflies are the fastest insects. They catch and eat other flying insects. They can even fly backwards!
pages.brief: A dragonfly hovers and darts above a pond, four wings spread, then flies backwards. It chases and catches other flying insects in mid-air. Birds, bats and insects all fly, and flying is a fast way to travel.

pages.text: The fastest animal on Earth is the peregrine falcon. It hunts other birds by diving on them from above. During a dive, it tucks in its wings and sails straight down.
pages.brief: A peregrine falcon dives from high above, wings tucked tight against its body, sailing straight down. It hunts other birds by dropping on them from above, reaching amazing speed during the dive.

pages.text: So Fast Cheetahs run as fast as a car. Sailfish swim faster than a motorboat. Falcons dive as fast as an airplane. Animals can reach amazing speeds!
pages.brief: A cheetah runs across grassland, a sailfish speeds through blue sea, and a peregrine falcon dives from the sky. Each animal reaches amazing speeds: fast as a car, faster than a motorboat, fast as an airplane.

books.title: Extreme Animals
books.art_why: Real animals exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Some animals like to be different! They are extreme animals. Many of these animals have special titles. They are the tallest. They are the fastest. They are the loudest. They move, eat, and make noise in different ways. This book tells many fun facts about these animals. A giraffe is as tall as a two-story house. A blue whale is as long as half of a football field. An elephant weighs as much as two pickup trucks. Biggest.
pages.brief: A tall giraffe stands beside a two-story house, a blue whale stretches alongside half a football field, and a heavy elephant is shown next to two pickup trucks. The animals are outdoors in open space, grouped to show their huge size and the different ways they move, eat, and make noise.

pages.text: Smallest One tiny type of monkey is as small as a mouse. A bee hummingbird weighs less than the water in a spoon. A Chihuahua is a little dog that can fit in your pocket. A blue whale’s cries are as loud as a rocket. Quietest A giraffe is quiet because it doesn’t use its voice. The screams of a howler monkey can be heard 8 kilometers (5 mi) away. Loudest.
pages.brief: A tiny monkey sits beside a mouse, a bee hummingbird balances near a spoon holding water, and a Chihuahua peeks out from a pocket. A blue whale sends out a loud cry near a rocket, while a giraffe stays silent and a howler monkey calls loudly.

pages.text: Longest Life A big land turtle can live for 150 years. One type of falcon dives as fast as an airplane flies. Shortest Life A mayfly lives for only one day. A garden snail will take a long time to crawl across your shoe. Slowest An ostrich can run as fast as a horse. A cheetah can run over 105 kilometers (65 mi) an hour. Fastest.
pages.brief: A big land turtle rests, a falcon dives through the sky, and a mayfly hovers for its one day. A garden snail crawls across a shoe, an ostrich runs like a horse, and a cheetah sprints at high speed across open ground.

pages.text: Fun Facts About Reptiles A snake never closes its eyes. A lizard can grow a new tail if it breaks off. A crocodile can hold its breath for an hour. Tiny sea horse babies stay inside their father’s body while they grow. The tongue of one big whale weighs as much as a small car. Fun Facts About Water Creatures.
pages.brief: A snake stares with eyes wide open, a lizard shows a new tail growing back, and a crocodile stays still holding its breath. A male seahorse carries tiny babies inside his body, while a huge whale tongue rests beside a small car.

pages.text: A camel can close its nose to keep out blowing sand. A kangaroo can balance on its tail. It can kick with all four feet. A mudskipper is an odd fish. It can skip out of the water and climb a tree. A halibut is flat. Both of its eyes are on the same side of its head. A big hippo can run faster than a person. Each zebra has a different pattern of stripes on its body. Fun Facts About Mammals.
pages.brief: A camel closes its nose in blowing sand, a kangaroo balances on its tail and kicks with four feet, and a mudskipper skips out of water to climb a tree. A flat halibut shows both eyes on one side, a hippo runs fast, and a zebra displays its own stripe pattern.

pages.text: Fun Facts About Insects A butterfly can taste food with its feet. A penguin uses its wings to swim fast. Penguins are not able to fly. A tiny hummingbird can fly backward. A cricket has ears on its knees. An ant can smell things just as well as a dog. The eye of an ostrich is larger than its brain. An eagle’s feathers weigh more than its bones do. Fun Facts About Birds.
pages.brief: A butterfly tastes food with its feet, a penguin swims fast using its wings, and a tiny hummingbird flies backward. A cricket shows ears on its knees, an ant sniffs like a dog, and an ostrich’s large eye sits beside its small brain. An eagle’s feathers are shown heavier than its bones.

books.title: Japan
books.art_why: Japan is a real country today with living cities, mountains and coastlines that photographs show, and the book describes modern Tokyo skyscrapers and busy streets.

pages.text: Japan Russia China North Korea SEA OF JAPAN (East Sea) PACIFIC OCEAN South Korea Tokyo Japan YELLOW SEA Japan ASIA Where Is It? Japan is made up of a group of islands in the Pacific Ocean. It is just off the east coast of Asia. Japan has four main islands and thousands of smaller islands. The entire country is smaller than the state of California.
pages.brief: A wide view from above of the Japanese islands, a long green chain ringed by blue sea. Four large islands and thousands of smaller ones lie in the Pacific Ocean, close to the coast of the Asian continent, with open ocean stretching all around them.

pages.text: Tokyo (TOH-kee-yoh) is the capital city of Japan. It is on the largest island, called Honshu (HON-shoo). Tokyo has many tall skyscrapers. More than thirty-two million people live there.
pages.brief: The city of Tokyo on the island of Honshu, filled with tall glass skyscrapers reaching into the sky. Crowds of people walk the streets below the towers and the city spreads far into the distance, home to more than thirty-two million people.

pages.text: People More than 127 million people live in Japan. The country’s main language is Japanese. More people live in cities and towns than in the country. City life in Japan is very busy. Most cities have little space, and people are crowded together.
pages.brief: A busy Japanese city street crowded with people walking shoulder to shoulder between close-set buildings. Homes and shops are packed tightly together with little open space, and in the distance more towns and city buildings cover the land.

pages.text: Most people in Japan eat rice. Japan grows much of the rice it uses. The Japanese also catch many fish and sell them across the world.
pages.brief: Japanese farmers standing in a green rice paddy, and beside them fishermen on a boat hauling a net full of silver fish from the sea. Baskets of rice and crates of fresh fish wait on the shore to be eaten and sold around the world.

pages.text: Land Most of Japan is covered with mountains. The country has more than seventy volcanoes. The most famous one is Mount Fuji (FOO-jee). It has not erupted in many years. Earthquakes are also common.
pages.brief: Mount Fuji, a huge cone-shaped volcano with a snowy peak, rising above green mountain forests. Rocky slopes around it show the many volcanoes of Japan, and cracked, shaking ground nearby shows that earthquakes are common here too.

Shikoku Kyushu Mts. EAST CHINA SEA Kyushu Ryukyu Islands PHILIPPINE SEA The land near the coast is the only flat land in Japan. Japan’s biggest cities are on the coasts. The country has many rivers and lakes.
pages.brief: Flat green land along the coast, where Japan's biggest cities sit close to the water. Behind them mountain ranges rise in long ridges across the islands, with rivers winding down between the peaks and small lakes lying in the valleys.

pages.text: Japanese Kanji fire mountain rain The Chinese characters borrowed by Japanese writing are called kanji (KAHN-jee). History Japan is thousands of years old. Ancient Japanese and Chinese people traded things and ideas. Some experts think that Japan learned to grow rice from China. Japanese writing even borrows from Chinese writing.
pages.brief: An ancient Japanese trader and a Chinese trader meeting on a shore, swapping bundles of goods and sharing ideas. Behind them farmers stand in a wet rice field tending young plants, and one trader holds a writing brush borrowed from Chinese writing.

pages.text: In the past, Japan was an empire. It was ruled by emperors. Later, powerful military leaders called shoguns (SHOH-guns) took control away from the emperors. Samurai (SA-muh-rye) warriors also had power. The samurai were known as brave and skilled fighters.
pages.brief: A samurai warrior in layered armour, helmet and sword, standing tall and looking brave and skilled. Nearby a powerful shogun gives orders, while an emperor in fine robes stands apart with no control, in Japan long before modern times.

pages.text: Celebrations The Japanese New Year is an important holiday in Japan. It starts a week before the first day of January. People send cards for the New Year’s holiday. They also clean their homes, and children often get gifts.
pages.brief: A Japanese family getting ready for the New Year. People clean their homes, wiping floors and windows, while children hold new gifts with happy faces. On a table nearby, New Year's cards wait to be sent a week before the first day of January.

pages.text: Food Rice is an important food in Japan. It is eaten at most meals. Noodles are also served with some meals. Another important food is fish. Japanese people sometimes eat raw fish called sushi (SOO-shee).
pages.brief: A table set with Japanese food: a bowl of white rice, a bowl of noodles, and pieces of fresh raw fish arranged as sushi. A family sits together to eat with chopsticks, rice served at most meals and fish an important food.

pages.text: Conclusion Japan is a small island country, yet it has many people. It has tall mountains and volcanoes. It also has crowded cities with skyscrapers. Japan is a mix of many things—old and new, large and small.
pages.brief: A crowded Japanese city of tall skyscrapers standing beside a huge volcano and high mountains, showing old and new together. Below, busy streets full of people; above, snowy peaks. A small island country holding many people and many different things.

books.title: France
books.art_why: Modern France, Paris, farms, mountains and French food all exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: France United Kingdom Belgium Germany English Channel Luxembourg Paris ATLANTIC OCEAN Dijon France Switzerland Limoges Bay of Biscay Italy Bordeaux Bayonne Toulouse Marseille Monaco Gulf of Lion EUROPE Spain Corsica ASIA AFRICA MEDITERRANEAN SEA Where Is It? France is a country in Europe. Other countries are to the east. To the south is Spain. The Atlantic Ocean is to the north and to the west. The United Kingdom is to the north. It is across a part of the Atlantic Ocean called the English Channel.
pages.brief: A wide view of Europe drawn as a simple map, with the shape of France in the middle. Spain sits below it, the Atlantic Ocean stretches to the west and north, the English Channel and the United Kingdom lie above, and other countries line the eastern side.

pages.text: Paris is the capital city of France. It is a very famous city. Millions of tourists visit Paris every year. More than ten million people live there.
pages.brief: A busy Paris street filled with tourists from many countries, some taking photographs, some walking in small groups and some sitting outside cafés. Tall pale stone buildings with iron balconies line the wide street, and crowds of people who live in the city move among them.

pages.text: People More than sixty-six million people live in France. Most people live and work in cities. Some have jobs helping tourists who visit France.
pages.brief: A crowded city street where adults hurry to work, carrying bags and entering office doors. Nearby, a guide stands with a small group of visitors, pointing out the sights, and other people work in shops and cafés serving the tourists who pass by.

pages.text: Some farmers in France grow flowers like these sunflowers. Some people live in the countryside and grow food on farms. More than half of the land in France is used for farming. Most people in France speak French.
pages.brief: A wide field of tall sunflowers in bright yellow bloom, their heads turned to the sun. A farmer walks between the rows in work clothes. Behind the field are green countryside, low farm buildings and vegetable plots, with a few houses far off.
