It has hills, forests, rivers, lakes, and beaches. Most of France is covered with low plains and hills.
pages.brief: A wide landscape showing many kinds of land: soft green plains and rolling hills, dark forests, a river winding through a valley, a small blue lake and a sandy beach at the edge of the sea, all under a bright sky.

pages.text: France also has five mountain ranges. They sit between France and other countries. The highest mountains are in the Alps.
pages.brief: Five separate mountain ranges shown rising between France and the countries around it, with rocky ridges and dark slopes. The tallest range, the Alps, stands in the east with high snow-covered peaks, sharp edges and deep valleys below.

pages.text: History Long ago, France was called Gaul. Other countries took over Gaul many times. The Romans took it over first, and then the Franks took it from the Romans. France got its name from the Franks.
pages.brief: Roman soldiers in armour and helmets marching into a walled settlement in Gaul, with carts and horses behind them. Later, Frankish warriors with spears and shields take over the same land, standing where the Romans once camped.

pages.text: For a long time, France was ruled by powerful kings. Then the French people fought against one king. This was called the French Revolution (1789–1799). Today, France is a democracy.
pages.brief: A powerful king in a rich robe and crown seated on a throne in a palace hall, with guards and nobles around him. In a crowded city square, ordinary French people in 1700s clothes gather together, raising their hands and protesting against the king.

pages.text: Celebrations People in France celebrate the beginning of the revolution on July 14. They celebrate with fireworks and parades.
pages.brief: Night over a French town, with bright fireworks bursting in the sky above the rooftops. Below, crowds of people line the streets and watch a parade of marchers in uniform and musicians pass by, cheering and clapping.

pages.text: Food France is known for its food. One type of food is a long, thin loaf of bread. Many meals have more than one part. A meal may have soup, salad, a main course, and fruit for dessert.
pages.brief: A table set with a long, thin loaf of bread beside a full meal: a bowl of soup, a fresh green salad, a main course on a plate and a dish of fruit for dessert. Hands reach in to serve, in a warm French kitchen.

pages.text: Conclusion France is a beautiful country with a long history. It has rolling hills, forests, and mountains. Its food is known around the world. What do you like most about France?
pages.brief: Rolling green hills and forests stretch across the countryside with mountains rising in the distance, and a table in the foreground holds a long loaf of French bread. The scene is calm and wide, showing the land and its food.

books.title: Model Rockets
books.art_why: Model rockets exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Liftoff! Watching these small rockets fly can be fun and exciting. Model rockets aren’t just for fun, though. They also teach us about science and space.
pages.brief: Small model rockets lift off and fly upward while people watch. The rockets are small but exciting to see, and the scene suggests that model rockets are not only fun but also help us learn about science and space.

pages.text: The History of Rockets People in China invented rockets about eight hundred years ago. They filled tubes with gunpowder and shot them at their enemies. Later, scientists built rockets that could go into space. Starting in the 1950s, people began building model rockets for fun.
pages.brief: People in China eight hundred years ago fill tubes with gunpowder and aim them at enemies. Later, scientists stand beside a rocket built to go into space. In a more recent scene, people in the 1950s build small model rockets for fun.

pages.text: Parts of a Model Rocket A model rocket kit comes with all the parts a rocket needs.
pages.brief: A model rocket kit is spread out on a table, showing the parts needed to build a rocket: a nose cone, a long body tube, fins, an engine, and a parachute, ready for assembly.

pages.text: Nose cones and rocket bodies come in many shapes and sizes. A model rocket’s body is a long tube made of cardboard or plastic. The nose cone fits into the top of the tube. The size and shape of a rocket’s body and nose cone can change how it flies.
pages.brief: Several model rocket bodies and nose cones are shown in different shapes and sizes. One long cardboard tube stands upright with a nose cone fitted on top; nearby are wider, narrower, shorter, and longer tubes and cones, showing how design can change flight.

pages.text: Steps in a Model Rocket’s Flight 4 The rocket engine makes a small upward explosion that pops the nose cone off, pulling the parachute out. 5 The parachute opens and slows the rocket’s fall. 3 The engine stops and the rocket coasts upward. 6 The rocket returns safely to Earth. 2 The engine pushes the rocket faster and higher. 7 The rocket touches down. Once the parachute is repacked and the engine is replaced, the rocket can fly again. 1 The engine starts and the rocket lifts off. Fins help the rocket fly straight. The engine burns fuel to push the rocket into the air. A parachute helps the rocket fall safely back to Earth.
pages.brief: A model rocket is shown at flight stages: the engine starts and the rocket lifts off; fins help it fly straight; the engine pushes it faster and higher, then stops and the rocket coasts upward. A small explosion pops the nose cone off, pulling out a parachute that opens, slows the fall, and lets the rocket touch down safely.

pages.text: People like to make their rockets look great. Many people paint their rockets with different colors and designs. Every rocket is one of a kind!
pages.brief: People decorate model rockets, painting them with bright colors and different designs. Several finished rockets stand side by side, each with its own color pattern and shape, showing that every model rocket can look one of a kind.

pages.text: At the Launchpad The only place to launch a rocket is in an open space. The launch area needs to be far away from people and buildings. A large field or a playground is a good spot. First, set up the launchpad. Place the rocket over the guide wire on the pad. The guide wire keeps the rocket pointing straight up when it lifts off. Connect the launch controller to the rocket engine. Then step back and press the button on the controller to start the engine. Whoosh! The rocket flies up and away.
pages.brief: In a large open field away from people and buildings, a person sets up a launchpad. They place a model rocket over the guide wire, connect the launch controller to the engine, then step back and press the button. The rocket lifts off straight up and flies away with a whoosh.

pages.text: Staying Safe Model rockets are fun, but they can be dangerous. Follow these rules to stay safe: • Use only safe materials and engines in your rocket. • Always launch your rocket outside in an open area. • Make sure there is no dry grass or any other fire hazard at the launch site. • Make sure everyone is at least 15 feet (4.5 m) away before you launch your rocket. • Count down before you launch. • Ask an adult for help if you have any questions.
pages.brief: A safe launch scene shows a model rocket on a launchpad in an open outdoor area with no dry grass or fire hazards. Everyone stands far back, at least fifteen feet away, while an adult helps. The group counts down together before launching, following safety rules.

pages.text: Clubs and Competitions People who fly model rockets often join model rocket clubs. Schools or hobby groups can have information about model rocket clubs. A science center or museum might have a model rocket club, too.
pages.brief: A model rocket club meets outdoors, with members holding their rockets and talking together. A school hobby group and a science center or museum are also shown as places where people can find out about model rocket clubs and join in.

pages.text: Many people enter model rocket competitions. They set off rockets and see which one flies the highest and the fastest. Model rocket competitions are held all over the world.
pages.brief: People at a model rocket competition set off their rockets and watch them climb, comparing which one flies highest and fastest. Other competition scenes show that these events are held in different places around the world.

pages.text: In the United States, students between twelve and eighteen can enter the Team America Rocketry Challenge. Every spring, one hundred teams compete to become the best in the country. The winners go on to compete against other teams from around the world.
pages.brief: Students between twelve and eighteen gather with their model rockets for the Team America Rocketry Challenge in the United States. One hundred teams compete in spring to be the best in the country. The winning team is shown with their rocket, preparing to compete against teams from around the world.

pages.text: Model rockets are a fun way to learn about science. Who knows how high a model rocket can take your imagination?
pages.brief: A child watches a model rocket soar high into the sky, imagining how far it can go. The scene suggests science learning and space, showing that model rockets are a fun way to learn and let imagination grow.

books.title: The Mighty Mississippi
books.art_why: The book is about a real river, real places, animals, and people, so photographs fit.

pages.text: The Mighty Mississippi.
pages.brief: A broad, winding river fills the view under an open sky, with water stretching toward the horizon and land along both banks. The scene shows the great Mississippi River as a single wide waterway, calm and powerful, with no people or boats in sight.

pages.text: Clouds gather above Minnesota’s Lake Itasca. A Long Journey Rain falls on Lake Itasca. It mixes into the clear waters of a river so small that a child could wade across it. So begins the mighty Mississippi River. A Lake of Many Names Lake Itasca is just one name for the lake where the Mississippi River begins. The Ojibwe people, who first lived in the area, called the lake Omashkoozo-zaaga’igan.
pages.brief: Dark clouds gather above Lake Itasca in Minnesota as rain falls onto the lake and its clear, shallow water. A tiny stream begins here, narrow enough that a child could wade across it. The surrounding land is quiet and natural, with the lake opening into the small river.

pages.text: Over the next three months, the water will take a 2,350-mile (3,781 km) journey through ten U.S. states. At last, it will reach the Gulf of Mexico. United States A watershed is the area that drains into a river or lake. The Mississippi River watershed is huge! It’s the fourth largest in the world. Many other rivers flow into the Mississippi. One of them— the Missouri—is even longer than the Mississippi!
pages.brief: An aerial view shows the Mississippi River watershed, with many rivers and streams flowing into the main river across a vast landscape toward the Gulf of Mexico. The water's long route appears as winding channels through green land, stretching far into the distance.

pages.text: The Upper River At first, the river flows through dozens of locks and dams. They work together to raise or lower the water around boats. The water levels change to allow boats to travel safely. They also hold back water so boats don’t hit the river bottom.
pages.brief: On the upper Mississippi River, a line of locks and dams spans the water. A boat waits in a lock as the water level changes around it. The dam holds back water, keeping the channel deep enough for boats to travel safely.

pages.text: Boats on this part of the river carry corn and soybeans south. Much of this food is shipped around the world.
pages.brief: On the river, long barges carry piles of corn and soybeans southward. The boats move along the wide waterway, loaded with farm crops. In the distance, a shipping area suggests the food will travel on around the world.

pages.text: More than fifty kinds of mammals live along the upper river. River otters love to play here. Oldies but Goodies At least 260 kinds of fish live in the Mississippi River. One kind is the pallid sturgeon, one of the oldest fish on Earth. It has hardly changed in 70 million years.
pages.brief: Along the upper river, river otters tumble and play at the water's edge. Beneath the surface, several kinds of fish swim, including a long pallid sturgeon with a pointed snout. The riverbank and clear water show a busy natural habitat.

pages.text: Farther down, a big, muddy river comes in from the west. It mixes with the clear waters of the Mississippi. The river grows brown and wide.
pages.brief: Farther down the Mississippi, a big muddy river flows in from the west. Its brown water mixes with the clearer water of the Mississippi. The joined river grows wide and brown as it continues across the land.

pages.text: For the next 190 miles (306 km), the river runs through areas with many wild animals. Bald eagles nest in the tall trees. They eat the fish that swim in the river.
pages.brief: For a long stretch of the river, tall trees line the banks. Bald eagles nest high in the branches, looking out over the water. Below, fish swim in the river, and the eagles watch for a meal.

pages.text: The Lower River Another big river joins the Mississippi from the east. The river grows deep and even wider. In many spots, it stretches 1.5 miles (2.4 km) across.
pages.brief: On the lower Mississippi, another big river joins from the east. The water grows deeper and even wider, stretching far across the landscape. In many places, the river is so wide that the far bank looks distant.

pages.text: With so much water, the Mississippi is famous for its floods. They can cause a lot of damage, but not all floods are bad. Along the river’s banks, the floods leave behind rich soil for farming.
pages.brief: The Mississippi River rises over its banks in a flood. Water spreads across low-lying land, and some damage is visible along the shore. When the flood pulls back, dark, rich soil remains on the nearby fields, ready for farming.

pages.text: More cities rise up here, and the boats carry iron, steel, rubber, and wood. They carry farm crops such as cotton from the area, too. Some things move north, back up the river, and some move farther south.
pages.brief: Cities rise along the lower river, with buildings near the water. Barges carry iron, steel, rubber, and wood, along with farm crops such as cotton. Some boats head north up the river, while others move farther south.

pages.text: Several types of turtles call this part of the river home. So do alligators! Swimming All Summer Even humans swim in the river sometimes. In the summer of 2002, Slovenian long-distance swimmer Martin Strel swam the entire length of the river, from Minnesota to Louisiana, in sixty-eight days.
pages.brief: In this part of the river, turtles rest on logs and alligators swim near the bank. A long-distance swimmer, Martin Strel, strokes through the open water during a long swim. The river stretches wide around him, with wildlife nearby.

pages.text: The Mighty Mississippi.
pages.brief: A final wide view shows the mighty Mississippi River flowing across the land under a broad sky. The water curves into the distance, wide and strong, with quiet banks on either side. The river fills the scene from foreground to horizon.

books.title: Yellowstone: A Place of Wild Wonders
books.art_why: The keyword check indicates drawing, so the book uses illustrated scenes of Yellowstone.

pages.text: Yellowstone: A Place of Wild Wonders.
pages.brief: A broad Yellowstone landscape opens the book, with open ground, distant hills, steamy hot pools, and a wide, empty sky. The quiet scene introduces a place of wild natural wonders, with no people anywhere in view.

pages.text: Steamboat Geyser bison hot spring Introduction Colorful pools and wild animals. Streams of hot water that shoot out of the ground. People can see these things and more at Yellowstone, which became the world’s first national park in 1872. National parks are areas of special, protected land.
pages.brief: A colorful hot spring steams beside a bison, while a geyser shoots hot water high into the open air. Visitors stand nearby, looking at the wild animals and steaming pools in Yellowstone, a protected national park.

pages.text: A Hot Spot Many people who go to Yellowstone want to see Old Faithful geyser. A geyser is a hole in the ground that shoots steam and hot water into the air. Yellowstone has about three hundred of them. Old Faithful shoots water 100 feet (30 m) high about every ninety minutes. Yellowstone Supervolcano Yellowstone is home to an old caved-in volcano. Over the past two million years, the volcano has had three big eruptions. The rim of the caved-in volcano is huge. It is more than 45 miles (72 km) across in some places. People still watch Yellowstone closely. The volcano doesn’t look as if it is going to erupt again soon.
pages.brief: Old Faithful erupts, sending hot water and steam high above the ground. Nearby, a wide view shows the rim of a huge caved-in volcano stretching across the land. Scientists watch the area closely, though the volcano does not seem ready to erupt soon.

pages.text: Yellowstone is on top of a hot spot. Heat from Earth’s center warms up rocks and rainwater in the ground. Then hot water and steam move up and shoot out of the ground. The hot spot has also made hot pools of smelly mud and many colorful hot springs.
pages.brief: Below Yellowstone, heat from deep inside Earth warms rocks and rainwater. Hot water and steam rise and burst out of the ground. Above, the hot spot creates colorful hot springs and pools of smelly mud across the surface.

pages.text: Wildlife Many kinds of animals live in Yellowstone. The biggest animals in Yellowstone are bison. They can weigh up to 2,000 pounds (907 kg). Bison are hairy animals with a hump on their back. They roll in the dust to fight off flies and to get rid of their old fur.
pages.brief: A large bison with a hump on its back rolls in the dust. Its thick, hairy coat is shedding old fur, and dust clouds rise around it. The bison is the biggest animal in Yellowstone, and rolling helps it fight off flies.

pages.text: The next-biggest animals are grizzly bears. They can weigh 800 pounds (363 kg) and are fast for their size. In the winter, grizzly bears sleep in dens under the ground for months.
pages.brief: A grizzly bear stands in Yellowstone, strong and fast for its size. In the distance, another grizzly sleeps in a den under the ground. The bears can weigh 800 pounds and spend months sleeping through winter.

pages.text: Settlers forced wolves out of Yellowstone over one hundred years ago. Later, workers for the national park brought them back. About one hundred wolves live in Yellowstone today.
pages.brief: A pack of wolves moves through Yellowstone. Long ago, settlers forced wolves out of the park, but park workers later brought them back. About one hundred wolves live in Yellowstone today, roaming the protected land.

pages.text: More than 350 other kinds of wild animals also live in the park. People may see elk, deer, golden eagles, fish, beavers, and foxes. Yellowstone is a safe place for them.
pages.brief: Elk, deer, a golden eagle, fish, a beaver, and a fox are shown in Yellowstone. More than 350 other kinds of wild animals live in the park. Yellowstone is a safe place for all these animals to live.

pages.text: History Native peoples hunted, fished, and gathered plants in Yellowstone. The geysers were also very important to their faith.
pages.brief: Native people hunt, fish, and gather plants in Yellowstone. Nearby, a geyser shoots steam and hot water into the air. The geysers are very important to their faith, and the people live and work in this land.

pages.text: Later, European explorers went to Yellowstone. After taking it from Native peoples, the United States decided that no one could own or sell the land. The first national park was born.
pages.brief: European explorers stand in Yellowstone, looking over the steaming land. After taking the land from Native peoples, the United States decided no one could own or sell it. This made Yellowstone the first national park.

pages.text: There are now over fifty national parks in the United States. Some protect special natural areas. Others protect places that are important to remember.
pages.brief: Across the United States, more than fifty national parks protect special places. Some parks preserve natural areas with wild land and animals. Others protect places that are important to remember, keeping their stories safe for people today.

pages.text: Conclusion About three million people come from all over to visit Yellowstone every year. They fish, hike, camp, watch wildlife, and visit the hot springs. In Yellowstone, people can see natural beauty unlike anything else.
pages.brief: About three million visitors come to Yellowstone each year. They fish, hike, camp, watch wildlife, and visit the hot springs. The people take in natural beauty unlike anything else, surrounded by the park's wild wonders.

pages.text: Now that Yellowstone is protected as a national park, it will always be around.
pages.brief: Yellowstone is now protected as a national park. Its wild land, hot springs, and animals can remain for the future. The park will always be around, a special place where nature is kept safe for people to see.

books.title: Sugar, Sugar, Everywhere
books.art_why: Real foods, drinks, people and health settings can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction What kind of sugary treats do you know of? Many people think of cookies and cakes. Sugar is in other foods, too.
pages.brief: A group of children sit around a table in a bright kitchen, looking at a plate of cookies and a slice of cake. Their faces show curiosity as they think about sugary treats, while other foods sit nearby on the table.

pages.text: What Is Sugar? Did you know sugar is in milk? Sugar is also in plant foods. Fruits have sugar. Vegetables have sugar, too. The white stuff in a sugar bowl is table sugar. Table sugar is different than sugar from fruits and vegetables.
pages.brief: A glass of milk, a sliced apple, a carrot, and a small bowl of white table sugar sit on a kitchen counter. A child's hands point to the milk and vegetables, comparing natural sugar in plant foods with table sugar.

pages.text: When we eat sugar, our body changes it into a simple sugar called glucose. Glucose goes into our blood. It is a source of energy for the body. We need it to stay alive.
pages.brief: A child sits at a table after eating a sweet snack, then stands and moves with energy in a sunny room. A faint, simple view of red blood flowing through the body suggests glucose traveling in the blood to give energy.

pages.text: Where Sugar Is Found The body can get all the glucose it needs from naturally sweet foods. Many foods from stores, though, have sugar added to them.
pages.brief: A grocery store produce aisle shows naturally sweet fruits and vegetables in bins. Nearby, a shopper holds a packaged food from a store shelf, looking at foods that may have sugar added to them.

pages.text: Pasta sauce and ketchup often have added sugar. Many low-fat foods have added sugar. Sugar is often used to replace fat in low-fat foods.
pages.brief: A kitchen counter shows a jar of pasta sauce, a bottle of ketchup, and several low-fat food packages. A person's hands compare the products, showing that sugar is often added to sauces, ketchup, and low-fat foods to replace fat.

pages.text: Breakfast cereal can have sugar, too. Many cereals have sugary treats added. Even cereals with plain flakes may have added sugar. How much sugar is in these breakfast cereals? 1 cup Grams of sugar Shredded Wheat 0g Toasted Oats 1g Corn Flakes 2g Crisp Rice 3g Raisin Bran 18g.
pages.brief: Several bowls of breakfast cereal sit on a kitchen table, including plain flakes and cereal with raisins and sugary pieces. Small piles of sugar beside the bowls range from tiny to large, showing that cereals can contain different amounts of sugar.

pages.text: Sugar and Health People need some sugar in their blood. It gives them the energy they need. But too much sugar in the blood can be bad. It can harm the body.
pages.brief: A child sits at a table with sugary foods, looking tired, while a parent watches with concern. The scene suggests that people need some sugar in their blood for energy, but too much sugar can be bad for the body.

pages.text: Over a long time, too much sugar in the blood can lead to problems with some parts of the body. The heart and other body parts might have to strain to work right. Do You Know? Some soda pop and fruit-flavored drinks have lots of added sugar. Sweet drinks make up almost half of the added sugar that some people eat and drink.
pages.brief: A person holds a hand over their heart while sitting in a quiet room, and a glass of soda and a fruit-flavored drink sit on the table nearby. The scene suggests that too much sugar over time can make the heart and body work harder.

pages.text: Making Healthy Choices People can avoid some health problems by avoiding added sugar. They can eat more natural food. Sweet fruits have no added sugars.
pages.brief: A family shops in a produce market, filling a basket with fresh fruits and vegetables. A parent points to whole natural foods, showing that people can choose foods with no added sugars and avoid some health problems.

pages.text: They can eat more homemade meals. They can try to use foods that do not have added sugars.
pages.brief: A family cooks together in a home kitchen, preparing a homemade meal with fresh ingredients. Bowls of vegetables and other whole foods sit on the counter, showing that people can choose homemade meals and foods without added sugars.

pages.text: People can also try to limit sweet treats when snacking. They can reach for fresh fruit or nuts instead of donuts and cookies.
pages.brief: A child reaches past a box of donuts and a plate of cookies toward a bowl of fresh fruit and a small dish of nuts on a kitchen counter. A parent smiles nearby, showing healthier snack choices.

pages.text: Sugar makes food taste sweet. It can help keep our bodies going. Too much added sugar, though, can harm our health. Natural foods are a great source of energy. Fresh fruits and vegetables taste good and are good for the body!
pages.brief: A bright table displays fresh fruits and vegetables beside a small bowl of sugar. A child and a parent sit together, smiling as they eat natural foods, showing that sugar makes food sweet but too much added sugar can harm health.

books.title: The Grand Canyon
books.art_why: The book includes ancient formation and 1800s exploration, so drawn scenes suit the historical parts.

pages.text: The Grand Canyon.
pages.brief: A wide, sweeping view of the Grand Canyon, with tall rock walls rising on both sides and a broad open sky above. The canyon stretches far into the distance, quiet and enormous, filling the whole scene with space and scale.

pages.text: Grand Grand THE CANYON CANYON CANYON.
pages.brief: Another wide view of the Grand Canyon from a different angle, showing long rock walls and a deep, open valley. The land looks vast and ancient, with no people in sight, only the canyon and the sky.

pages.text: A Canyon So Grand The Grand Canyon, located in the Arizona desert, is so big that it can be seen from space.
pages.brief: A view of the Grand Canyon in the Arizona desert, so huge that it can be seen from space. The canyon opens wide across the land, with deep rock walls and distant plateau edges under a clear sky.

pages.text: A canyon is a big, steep valley that is usually formed by a river. The Grand Canyon National Park covers about 1,900 square miles (4,921 sq km). In some places the canyon is more than a mile (1.6 km) deep. It can take two weeks to go through the canyon on a river raft.
pages.brief: A deep, steep canyon with a river running along its bottom. The canyon walls rise high above the water. A river raft travels through the narrow valley, small against the enormous rock walls and wide space.

pages.text: The Grand Canyon became a national park in 1919. National parks are special places. The land and the animals that live there are protected. Incredible Condors Don’t forget to look up! The Grand Canyon is home to giant birds called California condors. These birds almost died out. People caught the birds and kept them safe so they could have babies. Today there are over five hundred California condors living in the wild.
pages.brief: California condors soar high above the Grand Canyon national park. The giant birds spread broad wings over the protected land, with canyon walls and open sky below and around them. More condors can be seen in the distance.

pages.text: Formation Time and erosion helped form the Grand Canyon. Erosion happens when bits of the ground are worn away. For millions of years, the Colorado River ran over and wore away the earth until a canyon was made. The rocks at the bottom of the canyon are almost two billion years old.
pages.brief: The Colorado River runs through the Grand Canyon, wearing away the earth over millions of years. The river cuts between high rock walls, and old, deep rocks are visible near the bottom of the canyon.

pages.text: The Grand Canyon is striped with colors. The stripes are layers of sediment that settled on top of each other over many years. Each layer helps us learn how Earth has changed over time.
pages.brief: Close view of the Grand Canyon’s colorful rock walls, striped with layers of sediment stacked one on top of another. The bands of color run across the cliffs, showing the many layers that settled over time.

pages.text: Home in the Grand Canyon Native people who still live in the Grand Canyon include the Havasupai (hah-vuh-SOO-py), Navajo (NAH-vuh-hoh), Hualapai (WAH-luh-py), Hopi (HOH-pee), Zuni (ZOO-nee), and Apache (uh-PA- chee) tribes. Their lives are different from their relatives’ from long ago, but they have passed down many stories and traditions. Exploration People have lived in the Grand Canyon for at least twelve thousand years. Native groups have hunted, built homes, and grown food there. The area is still home to many tribes.
pages.brief: Native people of the Grand Canyon region share stories and traditions. Elders speak with children near canyon land where their people have hunted, built homes, and grown food for thousands of years. The scene shows present-day families and their deep connection to the place.

pages.text: In the 1850s, settlers did not know much about the Grand Canyon. In 1869, John Wesley Powell led a trip through the canyon. Local people taught him about the canyon’s history. Powell and his team were the first to write the history down.
pages.brief: In 1869, John Wesley Powell leads a team on a trip through the Grand Canyon. Local Native people teach him about the canyon’s history. Powell and his team listen and later write the history down, traveling through the steep canyon.

pages.text: When the government made the canyon a national park, it forced local tribes to leave. They were kept out for a long time. Today, some Native people help protect the canyon and its history. A Tale of Two Rims The South Rim of the Grand Canyon is very popular. It is open every day of the year. Across the canyon is the North Rim, which is a long drive away for most people. The North Rim is much higher up, so it gets more snow. It is only open in the warmer months of the year.
pages.brief: The South Rim of the Grand Canyon is shown open and popular, while the higher North Rim lies across the canyon with snow. Native people help protect the canyon and its history, standing near the rim as the two sides stretch apart.

pages.text: Make Your Own Adventure Today, millions of people visit Grand Canyon National Park. Some hikers explore the canyon for weeks.
pages.brief: Hikers with backpacks walk along a trail inside the Grand Canyon, exploring the huge landscape. Some hike for weeks, moving between tall rock walls and open views. The trail stretches ahead through the canyon.

pages.text: People like to raft on the Colorado River. It can be rough, fast, and rocky, making for a grand adventure.
pages.brief: People raft on the Colorado River in the Grand Canyon. The water is rough, fast, and rocky, splashing around the raft. Rafters hold on as they ride through the canyon walls on a grand adventure.

pages.text: People also love to walk on trails along the rim of the canyon. They can look out at miles of red and yellow walls and watch shadows move across the cliffs.
pages.brief: People walk on trails along the rim of the Grand Canyon. They look out over miles of red and yellow canyon walls. Shadows move across the cliffs as the walkers take in the wide view from the edge.

pages.text: A Natural Wonder The Grand Canyon is one of the most amazing sights in nature. Its land, peoples, animals, and history will be protected for years to come. Everyone who visits this national park is in for an adventure—and a view—unlike anything else.
pages.brief: A wide view of the Grand Canyon, one of nature’s most amazing sights. Visitors stand at an overlook, taking in the land, animals, peoples, and history protected in the national park. The canyon stretches out before them in every direction.

books.title: Russia
books.art_why: Russia is a real modern country with cities, people, and places that can be photographed.

pages.text: Russia FINLAND ESTONIA LATVIA BELARUS UKRAINE RUSSIA KAZAKHSTAN CHINA MONGOLIA EUROPE ASIA Where Is It? Russia is a very big country. It is the largest country in the world— almost twice as big as the United States. Russia is part of both Europe and Asia.
pages.brief: A broad view shows Russia as a very large landmass stretching across both Europe and Asia, with smaller neighboring countries around it. The land is shown larger than the United States, almost twice as big.

pages.text: Moscow is the capital of Russia. It is a big city in the European part of the country. More than twelve million people live there. The Russian president lives in a famous group of buildings in Moscow.
pages.brief: Moscow, a big city in the European part of Russia, is shown with busy streets and many people. A famous group of grand government buildings stands in the city, where the Russian president lives.

pages.text: People Most people in Russia live and work in cities. The main language is Russian. In the country, jobs have to do with the land and the sea. For example, many people fish, mine oil and coal, and cut trees for wood.
pages.brief: People in Russia are shown at work: city workers in busy streets, fishers at sea, miners beside oil and coal works, and tree cutters in forests. Most people live and work in cities, and the main language is Russian.

pages.text: Sports such as soccer and ice hockey are popular in Russia. Russia is famous for music and a kind of dance show called ballet. Swan Lake is a famous Russian ballet. Dancers perform Swan Lake. Russian teams play ice hockey.
pages.brief: Ballet dancers perform Swan Lake together on a stage, moving as a group. Nearby, Russian ice hockey players race across an ice rink with sticks, and soccer players play a match on a grassy field.

pages.text: Russia’s Landforms Moscow Land The land in Russia is mainly low flatlands, high flatlands, and mountains. The deepest lake in the world, Lake Baikal, is in Russia. Russia has frozen flatlands in the north and wide grassy lands in the south. In between are huge forests.
pages.brief: A wide Russian landscape shows low flatlands, high flatlands and mountains. Lake Baikal lies deep among the land. Frozen flatlands stretch in the north, wide grassy lands in the south, and huge forests fill the land between.

pages.text: Russia is a cold country, and it is home to the coldest village in the world. But many places in Russia also have beautiful summers.
pages.brief: Russia is shown as a cold country with a snowy village, the coldest village in the world. In another place, a beautiful summer scene has green land, open sky and warm light, showing that many parts of Russia also have lovely summers.

pages.text: History In the past, czars, or emperors, ruled Russia. During that time, the peasants in Russia were unhappy. They didn’t like the way the czars ruled the people. They fought in 1917 to change their country’s ways.
pages.brief: In the past, a Russian czar, or emperor, rules over unhappy peasants. The peasants do not like the way the czars rule the people. They gather and fight in 1917 to change their country’s ways.

pages.text: After the fight, Russia took control of a group of other nearby countries. Together they formed the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR). The USSR had many problems, so it broke up in 1991. Today, Russia has a president.
pages.brief: After the fight, Russia takes control of a group of nearby countries, and together they form the USSR. The USSR is shown with many problems, then it breaks up in 1991. Today, Russia has a president.

pages.text: Celebrations Many people celebrate Christmas and Easter in Russia. On Easter, they eat cakes and paint hard-boiled eggs. Russians also have a holiday to celebrate the end of winter. For this holiday, people eat pancakes with butter. They also have fun with sleigh rides and snowball fights.
pages.brief: Families celebrate Christmas and Easter in Russia. On Easter, they eat cakes and paint hard-boiled eggs. For a holiday marking the end of winter, people eat pancakes with butter, enjoy sleigh rides and have snowball fights.

pages.text: Food A popular soup in Russia is famous around the world. People make the soup from beets and other vegetables. Beets are red, so the soup also has a red color. Many Russians like a homemade drink. The drink has a sour flavor.
pages.brief: A popular Russian soup is shown in a bowl, made from red beets and other vegetables, so the soup has a red color. Beside it, a homemade Russian drink is served in a cup, and it has a sour flavor.

pages.text: Conclusion Russia is home to both crowded cities and wild forests. Russia has a long, rich history and many interesting things to do. The Russian people value the traditions of their beautiful homeland.
pages.brief: Today, Russia is shown with both crowded cities and wild forests, along with a long, rich history. The Russian people value the traditions of their beautiful homeland, and there are many interesting things to do.

books.title: South Korea
books.art_why: The book includes maps and historical scenes that are best shown as drawings.

pages.text: South Korea CHINA NORTH KOREA SOUTH KOREA Where Is It? South Korea is a country in East Asia. It is close to China. The closest country to South Korea is North Korea. RUSSIA JAPAN.
pages.brief: A simple map view of East Asia shows the Korean peninsula, with South Korea beside North Korea. China lies to the west, Russia to the north, and Japan to the east. South Korea sits in East Asia, close to China and nearest to North Korea.

pages.text: The capital of South Korea is Seoul, the country’s largest city. Over nine million people live there. It is one of the largest cities in the world. Downtown Seoul has walls built more than six hundred years ago. The area contains many buildings from an earlier time.
pages.brief: A busy downtown Seoul scene shows many people among old buildings from an earlier time. An old stone wall built more than six hundred years ago stands in the area. Seoul is the capital and largest city, with over nine million people living there.

pages.text: People Many South Koreans speak Korean. Some people in Korea speak Chinese, Japanese, or English. South Koreans have many different types of jobs. They make cars, ships, and other things to sell in different countries. South Korea also has many computer jobs.
pages.brief: South Korean workers are shown in different jobs: making cars in a factory, building ships in a shipyard, and working at computers in an office. Nearby, a group of South Korean people talk together, using Korean and some Chinese, Japanese, or English.

pages.text: Family is important to Korean people. South Koreans keep careful family records. School is important as well. Korean parents work hard to help their children learn.
pages.brief: A Korean family sits together with careful family records, showing that family is important. In a classroom, Korean parents work hard to help their children learn with schoolwork, showing that school is important as well.

pages.text: Land Most of South Korea has hills and mountains. The highest peak is Mount Halla, an old volcano, at 1,950 meters (6,398 ft.).
pages.brief: Most of South Korea is shown as hills and mountains. Mount Halla rises as the highest peak, an old volcano reaching 1,950 meters, or 6,398 feet. The mountain landscape fills the view with slopes and high ground.

pages.text: Much of the coast of South Korea is broken up by rivers and streams. The land along the coast is very low. Most people in South Korea’s countryside live on the plains. Farmers there grow rice, fruits, and vegetables.
pages.brief: Much of South Korea's coast is broken up by rivers and streams, with very low land along the shore. In the countryside plains, farmers grow rice, fruits, and vegetables. The scene shows low coastal land, flowing water, and farm fields where people work.

pages.text: History For hundreds of years, Korea was a hard place to get to. Different kingdoms took control of the land. Japan took control of Korea in 1905, and did not give Korean people many freedoms. It remained under Japan’s control until the end of World War II.
pages.brief: A historical drawing shows Korea as a hard-to-reach land divided among kingdoms. Japanese officials take control in 1905, and Korean people live with limited freedoms. The scene continues until the end of World War II, when Japan's control ends.

pages.text: When the war ended, Korean people wanted to have their own government. The Soviet Union took control of North Korea. The United States supported South Korea. There was a war between the two sides. After the war South Korean people freely chose their leaders. North Korea had a leader put in place.
pages.brief: A divided Korean peninsula scene shows the Soviet Union controlling North Korea and the United States supporting South Korea. Fighting breaks out between the two sides. After the war, South Korean people freely choose their leaders, while a leader is put in place in North Korea.

pages.text: Holidays The Korean New Year festival called Seollal is an important celebration. On this holiday, people celebrate becoming one year older. The Korean festival called Chuseok is another important holiday. Families visit family graves. They remember their family members.
pages.brief: On Seollal, the Korean New Year festival, people celebrate becoming one year older. On Chuseok, another important holiday, families visit family graves and remember their family members. The scene shows both a joyful New Year celebration and a quiet family grave visit.

pages.text: Food Korean food has lots of flavor. A vegetable dish called kimchi and rice are served at most meals. Many South Koreans think food is the answer to good health. They believe what they eat can keep them from getting sick.
pages.brief: A Korean meal shows a vegetable dish called kimchi and rice served together, with lots of flavor. South Korean people believe food is the answer to good health and that what they eat can keep them from getting sick. The table is filled with these everyday foods.

pages.text: Conclusion South Koreans have shared the ideas of hard work and love of family for many years. Today, South Korea is a modern world power with a bright tomorrow.
pages.brief: A modern South Korean city shows a world power with a bright tomorrow. Families and workers share ideas of hard work and love of family that South Koreans have held for many years. The scene looks toward the future while honoring those long-held values.

pages.text: Population: 51,715,162 Land: 99,720 sq km (38,502 sq. mi.) Capital City: Seoul Primary Language: Korean Primary Religions: Christianity, Buddhism Name of Currency: Won.
pages.brief: A summary view of South Korea today shows Seoul's city skyline and many people, reflecting a population of over fifty-one million. A church and a Buddhist temple stand for the main religions. Coins and notes show the won, the country's currency, and Korean people talk together.

books.title: All About Snakes
books.art_why: Snakes are real animals that exist today, so photographs fit best.

pages.text: All About Snakes.
pages.brief: Several snakes of different sizes and colors rest among rocks and grasses in a natural outdoor setting, their bodies curved and still. One lifts its head slightly while the others stay coiled, giving a clear first view of snakes in the wild.

pages.text: All About All About Snakes Snakes.
pages.brief: A single snake lies stretched across warm ground beside low plants, its patterned scales catching the light. Around it are small stones and dry leaves, and the snake remains calm and still in the open.

pages.text: Introduction Some people do not like snakes. They may think snakes are gross or dangerous. Some can be dangerous. Snakes can also be beautiful and amazing.
pages.brief: A beautiful, brightly patterned snake rests on a rock in a garden, while a few people stand farther back with uneasy faces. The snake stays calm and still, showing both the beauty of snakes and some people’s fear of them.

pages.text: Where Snakes Live KEY Land snakes Sea snakes Some sea snakes can stay underwater for up to eight hours. They can also breathe through their skin! banded sea krait Where Do Snakes Live? Many snakes live on land. Some snakes live in or near bodies of water. Snakes cannot live where it is cold all year long. Snakes do not live on some islands.
pages.brief: A banded sea krait swims underwater, its striped body moving through the water. Nearby, a land snake rests at the edge of a pond. Far away, a snow-covered shore shows a cold place where snakes cannot live all year.

pages.text: A snake lies in the sun to warm its body. When it gets too warm, it goes in the shade or underground. Snake Traits Snakes are reptiles. All reptiles are cold-blooded and have a backbone. The body temperature of cold-blooded animals changes with their surroundings. They control their body temperature by moving to warmer or cooler places.
pages.brief: A green snake lies stretched on a sunlit rock, warming its body. Shade from a nearby plant and a small opening in the ground show where it can move when it gets too warm. Its long, legless body rests in the open.

pages.text: Snakes that live in places with cold winters hibernate. They go underground or beneath things where the temperature stays the same. The snakes do not move until the temperature warms again. Snakes that live where it is warm all year do not hibernate.
pages.brief: A snake lies coiled underground beneath roots and rocks, still and unmoving in cold winter conditions. Above the ground, bare branches and snow suggest the cold season. In a separate warm, sunny spot, another snake is active instead of hibernating.

pages.text: Snakes do not have legs, and their bodies are covered with scales. They move by pushing their bodies against a surface. The scales help grip the surface.
pages.brief: A close view of a snake’s scaly body pressing against rough ground, its scales gripping the surface as it moves. The snake has no legs, and its long body bends and pushes against the surface to help it shift forward.

pages.text: A snake’s skin does not grow with the snake. As a snake grows, its skin stretches and splits, showing new skin and scales beneath. The snake sheds its old skin and leaves it behind.
pages.brief: A snake is shown partway out of its old, split skin, leaving the thin, crumpled covering caught on a rock. The new skin and scales underneath look fresh and bright. The shed skin remains behind as the snake moves forward.

pages.text: Most snakes lay eggs with soft shells. These snakes lay eggs where they can hatch safely. Other snakes carry their eggs in their bodies. The eggs hatch in their bodies, and the baby snakes come out!
pages.brief: A female snake rests beside a hidden clutch of soft-shelled eggs under leaves, keeping them safe. Nearby, another snake’s body carries eggs inside, and tiny baby snakes are shown coming out from her body into the world.

pages.text: What Do Snakes Hunt, and How? All snakes eat other animals. Snakes use their tongues to find their prey. They stick out their tongues to “taste” the air. They follow the taste like a dog following a smell. Some snakes also have special body parts that can sense heat from other animals.
pages.brief: A snake moves through grass with its tongue sticking out, tasting the air as it hunts. Small animals are hidden nearby in the undergrowth. The snake’s head is raised slightly, following the scent and searching for prey.

pages.text: When snakes find their prey, some just bite and hold it. They may bite with their fangs or hold the prey in their jaws. Do Snakes Have Ears? The answer is “kind of.” Snakes do not hear like humans. However, they can feel some sounds through special parts of their head. One thing snakes don’t have is eyelids!
pages.brief: A snake bites and holds a small prey animal in its jaws, its fangs visible. A close view of the snake’s eye shows no eyelid. Its head rests near the ground, as if feeling sounds through special parts of its head.

pages.text: Some snakes coil around prey and squeeze until it is dead. Some snakes have strong venom that they inject into prey through a bite. The venom may slow, stop, or even kill the other animal.
pages.brief: A large constrictor coils tightly around a prey animal, squeezing it. Nearby, a venomous snake bites another small animal, its fangs injecting venom. Both scenes take place in a natural outdoor setting with grass, stones, and low plants around them.

pages.text: Most snakes cannot chew. Instead, they swallow their meal whole. Some snakes’ jaws open so wide that they can swallow prey larger than their head! A Snake’s Meal Once a snake eats, it rests. It can take days for a snake to break down its food. For large snakes that eat large prey, it can take weeks!
pages.brief: A snake stretches its jaws wide and swallows a whole meal larger than its head. After eating, it lies resting on the ground, its body swollen from the food. The snake stays still while its meal slowly breaks down over days.

pages.text: Conclusion Now that you know more about snakes, what do you think of them?
pages.brief: A snake rests in a natural outdoor setting, its head lifted and turned toward the viewer. Its patterned scales and calm pose fill the scene. Around it are low plants and stones, inviting people to think about what they know about snakes.

books.title: Migrating Geese
books.art_why: Real migrating geese and their habitats exist today.

pages.text: When the days get shorter, the geese fly south. When the temperatures get colder, the geese fly south. When the leaves fall from the trees, the geese fly south. It is fall, and winter will soon arrive. The land will be covered with snow and ice.
pages.brief: Several geese fly south across an autumn landscape. The trees have lost their leaves, and the air looks colder. The geese are high in the sky, heading away as fall turns toward winter, with land below that will soon be covered by snow and ice.

pages.text: The geese fly south in groups called flocks. They go to a warmer place. They take to the sky, and they get into formations shaped like the letter V. They head for a warmer place. They are migrating. Flying in a V-formation helps the geese to fly long distances. The V-formation makes it easier for the geese to move through the air. They can cut through the air like a knife.
pages.brief: A flock of geese flies south in a V-formation. The geese are high in the sky, moving together toward a warmer place. Their formation is shaped like the letter V as they travel long distances through the air.

pages.text: The goose in the front of the formation has to work the hardest. The geese take turns flying in the front. When the goose in front gets tired, a goose from the back takes its place. This is how geese in a flock work together. Sometimes a goose in a flock gets injured and has to stay behind. Another goose stays behind with the injured goose. It stays until the injured goose gets better.
pages.brief: In the sky, one goose leads the V-formation at the front. Another goose moves from the back to take its place. Below, an injured goose rests on the ground while a second goose stays beside it, waiting until the injured goose gets better.

pages.text: When the injured goose gets better, it continues to migrate. The other goose that stayed behind migrates, too. Geese are like a family. They take care of each other. If one goose needs help or is in danger, other geese are there to help.
pages.brief: The recovered goose and the goose that stayed behind fly together again, joining other geese in the sky. The flock continues migrating. The geese stay close and take care of one another like a family, with other geese nearby ready to help if one needs help or is in danger.

pages.text: The migrating geese find a warmer place. They find a place where lakes and rivers are not frozen. They find a place where the land is not covered with snow. They find a place where there is plenty of food to eat. They stay until the days in the north begin to get longer once again. They stay until the temperatures in the north get warmer once again. They stay until the trees in the north begin to leaf out and the grass begins to grow.
pages.brief: The migrating geese reach a warmer place with lakes and rivers that are not frozen. The land has no snow, and there is plenty of food. The geese stay in this warmer place until the days in the north grow longer and the trees begin to leaf out.

pages.text: Once again it is time to migrate. But this time the geese fly north. It is spring. In the north, the snow and the ice have melted. Food is plentiful, and spring has arrived.
pages.brief: The geese fly north once more across the sky. It is spring, and the snow and ice in the north have melted. The geese travel through a spring landscape where food is plentiful and spring has arrived.

pages.text: The geese mate and build a nest. The female lays eggs. Soon there will be baby geese. The baby geese have hatched. They are called goslings. Their parents will care for them and teach them to fly. Soon it will be time to migrate again.
pages.brief: A pair of adult geese stay near a nest on the ground. The female is close to eggs in the nest, and small goslings are beside the parents. The parents care for the young geese and will teach them to fly before it is time to migrate again.

books.title: Extreme Insects
books.art_why: Real insects, body traits, and natural habitats can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction Insects are always in danger. They have many enemies. They are food for each other as well as other animals.
pages.brief: A natural outdoor scene with many kinds of insects moving among leaves, soil, and stones, showing them as small creatures surrounded by danger. Some insects hide while others are close to larger animals that might eat them, illustrating that insects are food for one another and for other animals.

pages.text: Insects have many traits that help them stay alive. These traits include size, looks, and weapons. Let’s look at some of the extreme traits insects have that help them.
pages.brief: A group of different insects in a garden or meadow, each showing a different survival trait: one is very small, one has striking colors or shape, and one has a weapon-like body part. They sit among plants, as if being observed to see how these extreme traits help them stay alive.

pages.text: Extreme Size This beetle can grow as long as a pen. It can weigh as much as a banana. Extreme size and a hard cover protect it from its enemies.
pages.brief: A large beetle with a hard, dark cover resting on a leaf or log. Beside it are a pen and a banana, showing the beetle can be as long as the pen and as heavy as the banana. Its hard shell is visible as protection from enemies.

pages.text: This insect can grow longer than a new pencil. Its size frightens smaller insects away. Animals don’t eat it because they think it is just a big stick.
pages.brief: A very long, thin insect that looks like a stick standing on a branch among twigs and leaves. A new pencil lies nearby for comparison. Smaller insects keep their distance, while a larger animal looks toward it as if it thinks the insect is just a big stick.

pages.text: Extreme Look-Alikes Many insects look like other things. Their looks help them hide from animals that want to eat them.
pages.brief: Several insects in a leafy outdoor setting, each resembling something else in its surroundings. One blends into a leaf, another into a flower or stem, showing how their looks help them hide from animals that want to eat them.

pages.text: Some insects look like parts of plants. They can look like leaves, flowers, stems, or even thorns.
pages.brief: Close view of insects that look like plant parts: one shaped like a leaf, one like a flower, one like a stem, and one like a thorn. They rest on plants in a garden or forest, blending in so closely that their body shapes match the plant around them.

pages.text: There are insects with large fake eyes to scare hungry animals away. When scared, this caterpillar can make itself look like a snake.
pages.brief: A caterpillar on a branch, rearing up and puffing out parts of its body to show large fake eye spots. Its pose makes it resemble a small snake, frightening away a hungry animal nearby. The setting is a natural leafy place with twigs and foliage.

pages.text: Extreme Weapons Some insects have extreme weapons to help them survive. Some of these insects use their weapons to get food. Others use their weapons to keep from becoming food.
pages.brief: A collection of insects in a natural setting, each showing a different extreme body weapon, such as oversized mouthparts or a sharp pointed part. Some are hunting for food, while others face larger animals and use their weapons to avoid becoming food.

pages.text: This insect digs a pit in the sand. It traps ants in the pit. Then it grabs an ant in its large, sharp jaws. Yummy!
pages.brief: An insect at the edge of a small pit dug in sandy ground. An ant has fallen into the pit, and the insect waits with large, sharp jaws ready to grab it. The sandy pit is a trap, and the ant is caught inside.

pages.text: This bug jumps on other insects. It stabs them with its sharp beak. It shoots out poison that turns their insides to goo. Then the bug sucks out the goo. Slurp!
pages.brief: A bug leaping onto another insect in a natural outdoor setting. It stabs the other insect with a sharp beak and shoots out poison, while the other insect becomes gooey. The bug then sucks out the goo, showing how it uses its weapon to get food.

pages.text: Watch out! This beetle sprays out boiling hot poison when touched. It stops animals from trying to eat it.
pages.brief: A beetle on a leaf or ground, spraying hot, steaming poison from its body toward an animal that has touched it. The animal backs away, showing how the boiling hot spray stops animals from trying to eat the beetle.

pages.text: Conclusion Insects have many ways to protect themselves. Their size, color, and weapons can help them stay alive.
pages.brief: A wide natural scene with many insects of different sizes and colors, some with hard covers, some hidden among plants, and some showing weapon-like body parts. They are all surviving in their habitat, showing how size, color, and weapons help them stay alive.

books.title: Where We Get Energy
books.art_why: The book shows real energy sources, machines, places and everyday objects that can be photographed.

pages.text: Where We Get Energy.
pages.brief: A large glowing sun shines in a bright clear sky above open ground. Strong rays spread outward, filling the scene with light. The view is wide and simple, with no people or buildings, showing natural light as a powerful presence.

pages.text: Introduction We use energy for many of the things we do every day. Energy lights, heats, and cools our homes and schools. Energy is part of everything we do. You need energy to run and play. You need energy to think and sleep. Where does this energy come from?
pages.brief: A warm family home and a school building stand side by side, with glowing lights and comfortable rooms. Nearby, children run and play outdoors, then one child rests asleep in bed. The scene shows everyday places and actions that use energy.

pages.text: Energy comes from many kinds of important natural resources. Sunlight is our most important natural resource. Coal, natural gas, and oil are natural resources, too. So are things like plants, wind, and water.
pages.brief: Bright sunlight falls across plants, wind moves through trees, and clear water flows in a stream. Nearby, chunks of coal, containers of natural gas and oil are shown beside leafy plants. These natural resources appear together in one wide outdoor scene.

pages.text: Energy from Food Sources You get energy from foods you eat. Animals you eat may get energy from the plants they eat. Plants use energy from the Sun to make their own food. Plants can store the food they make in roots, stems, and leaves.
pages.brief: A child eats food at a table. In a sunny field, animals graze on green plants, and plants stand with their roots, stems, and leaves visible. Sunlight falls on the plants, showing how food and energy are connected.

pages.text: Energy from Gasoline Most cars, trucks, planes, and trains get energy from gasoline. Gasoline is made from oil. Oil is a natural resource found deep underground. Wells pump oil up from the ground. Factories change the oil into gasoline.
pages.brief: Cars, trucks, an airplane, and a train move on roads, in the sky, and on tracks. In the background, an oil well pumps oil up from deep underground, and a factory stands nearby. The factory changes the oil into gasoline for these vehicles.

pages.text: Electricity Electricity is a kind of energy. We use electricity to run many things that we use every day. How do we get electricity?
pages.brief: Inside a bright home, lamps glow, a refrigerator hums, and a television screen is on. Nearby, a computer and a fan use electric power. The scene shows many everyday objects that run on electricity, inviting the question of where electricity comes from.

pages.text: Making Electricity We can get electricity from a generator. A generator is a machine with huge blades that spin to make energy. A large power plant near your town may have many generators. Many kinds of fuel are used to run the generators.
pages.brief: A large power plant stands near a town, with many generators inside. One generator is shown close up, with huge blades spinning fast to make energy. Fuel feeds the generators as they work, and the plant connects to the town nearby.

pages.text: Energy from Coal About half the energy used to run generators comes from burning coal. Coal is a natural rock resource that is usually mined under the ground. Power plants can burn coal to make energy to heat water. Burning coal also causes pollution.
pages.brief: Coal is mined underground, with dark rock visible in a mine. At a power plant, coal burns to heat water, and smoke rises from the plant. The scene shows the rock resource, the burning process, and the pollution that comes with it.

pages.text: When water gets hot enough, it turns to steam. Flowing steam makes the fan blades inside a steam generator spin fast. Generators use energy made by the spinning blades to make electricity.
pages.brief: Hot water turns into steam inside a steam generator. The flowing steam rushes past fan blades, making them spin fast. The spinning blades turn the generator, and electricity is made inside the machine. The view shows the hot water, steam, and moving blades.

pages.text: Energy from Wind Wind can be used to make electricity. Blowing wind turns the large blades of a wind generator. The generator uses energy from the spinning blades to make electricity. Electricity from wind does not make any pollution.
pages.brief: A wind generator stands in an open, breezy field. Blowing wind turns its large blades, and the spinning blades make electricity inside the generator. The clear sky and clean landscape show that electricity from wind does not make pollution.

pages.text: Energy from Water Moving water can be used to make electricity. People build dams to block rivers. Water from a river moves through large pipes in the dam. The moving water spins the blades of the generators.
pages.brief: People stand near a large dam that blocks a river. Water from the river moves through large pipes in the dam, and the moving water spins the blades of generators inside. The scene shows the dam, the flowing water, and the generators making electricity.

pages.text: Energy from the Earth Some places under the earth are very hot. They have layers of hot rock and hot water deep underground. Hot steam rises out of holes in the ground. The steam is trapped in pipes and used to spin the blades of a generator.
pages.brief: Deep underground, layers of hot rock and hot water glow with heat. Hot steam rises out of holes in the ground above. The steam is trapped in pipes and sent to spin the blades of a generator, making electricity from the hot earth.

pages.text: Energy from the Sun People can use the Sun’s energy to make electricity. Solar cells and solar panels can change sunlight into electricity. Solar cells make this car move!
pages.brief: Solar panels stand under bright sunlight, changing the Sun's energy into electricity. Nearby, a car covered with solar cells sits on a sunny road, ready to move. The scene shows sunlight powering the panels and the car without any fuel.

pages.text: Switching Energy People use more energy each year. We use lots of coal, oil, and natural gas to run our cars, homes, and businesses. These natural resources can’t last forever, and they pollute the Earth.
pages.brief: People drive cars, use homes, and work in busy businesses, using more energy each year. Coal, oil, and natural gas are shown fueling these activities. Smoke and pollution spread around the scene, showing that these resources cannot last forever and pollute the Earth.

pages.text: Sun and wind are good energy resources to use instead. They don’t pollute, and they last forever.
pages.brief: Bright sunlight shines over solar panels while wind turns a wind generator in a clean landscape. The Sun and wind provide energy without smoke or pollution. The open sky and green ground show these resources lasting and keeping the Earth clean.

books.title: Gorillas
books.art_why: Gorillas, forests, Koko, and Francine are real and can be photographed.

pages.text: Gorillas Gorillas are members of the great- ape family. They live in the forests of Africa. Some gorillas live high up in the mountains. Others live in lowlands.
pages.brief: Several gorillas move through the wide green forests of Africa. Some stand among tall lowland trees, while others climb on a high mountain slope. The gorillas live and travel in these different African forest homes.

pages.text: Gorillas have strong, heavy bodies. They are the largest primates in the world. Monkeys, chimpanzees, and humans are primates, too.
pages.brief: A large gorilla stands with a strong, heavy body, showing it is the biggest primate. Nearby are a monkey, a chimpanzee, and a human, each with a primate body. The gorilla’s size stands out among them.

pages.text: Gorillas can walk on two legs, as people do. Most of the time, they walk on their feet and hands. This type of walking is called knuckle-walking.
pages.brief: One gorilla walks upright on two legs, as people do. Another gorilla leans forward and walks on its feet and hands, pressing its knuckles to the ground. The two ways of moving are shown in the forest.

pages.text: Gorillas mostly eat leaves, stems, bark, fruits, flowers, and wood. Some gorillas also eat snails and insects such as ants and termites. Gorillas build nests in trees or sleep on the ground. They never sleep more than one night in the same nest. They travel to different areas in search of food.
pages.brief: A gorilla eats leaves, stems, bark, fruits, flowers, and wood in the forest. Ants and termites crawl nearby, and snails rest on the ground. Another gorilla sleeps in a tree nest, while a ground nest sits below; the gorillas travel to new areas for food.

pages.text: Gorilla Families A gorilla family is called a troop or band. A troop eats, sleeps, and plays together. Family members wrestle and play tag and catch for fun. They groom each other’s fur. Grooming is an important way for them to be close and friendly together.
pages.brief: A gorilla family stays together in a troop, eating, sleeping, and playing. Two gorillas wrestle and chase each other in play, while another pair grooms each other’s fur. The grooming shows closeness and friendship among the family members.

pages.text: A gorilla baby nurses and stays close to its mother for a few years. It rides on her back to move around.
pages.brief: A mother gorilla holds her baby close and nurses it. The young gorilla stays near her for a few years. Later, the baby rides on its mother’s back as she moves through the forest, keeping the little gorilla close.

pages.text: When a male gorilla grows up, some of the fur on his back turns silver. The male is then called a silverback. The silverback’s job is to protect the troop.
pages.brief: A grown male gorilla stands with silver fur on his back, showing he is a silverback. Behind him, the gorilla troop stays together. The silverback watches over the others, ready to protect the troop in the forest.

pages.text: Gorillas Show How They Feel Sometimes, gorillas’ faces show how they feel. Their faces can show if they are happy, sad, or upset. Gorillas make crying sounds when they are upset. They make laughing sounds when they are tickled.
pages.brief: A gorilla’s face shows a happy, sad, or upset feeling. One gorilla makes crying sounds with an upset face. Another gorilla is being tickled and makes laughing sounds. Their faces and sounds show how they feel.

pages.text: Gorillas have other ways to communicate. They whimper, scream, bark, and grunt. They even use smells to silently warn other gorillas of danger.
pages.brief: Gorillas communicate with whimpers, screams, barks, and grunts. One gorilla grunts while another barks, and their sounds carry through the forest. Nearby, gorillas use smells to silently warn each other of danger, without making a sound.

pages.text: A woman named Francine taught a gorilla to use sign language. The gorilla’s name was Koko. Koko used signs to tell Francine what she wanted and how she felt.
pages.brief: Francine, a woman, sits with a gorilla named Koko. Koko uses sign language with her hands to tell Francine what she wants and how she feels. Francine watches the gorilla’s signs as Koko communicates with her.

pages.text: Gorilla Smarts Gorillas are very smart. They can make and use tools, but this doesn’t happen very often. A gorilla can use a twig to “fish” for ants. A gorilla can use a stick to check how deep a pool of water is. A gorilla can use a rock as a hammer to break open nuts.
pages.brief: A gorilla uses a twig to fish for ants. Another gorilla checks how deep a pool of water is with a stick. A third gorilla uses a rock as a hammer to break open nuts. These smart gorillas make and use simple tools.

pages.text: Gorillas in Danger Many gorillas have been killed by hunters. Their forest homes are being cut down. Gorillas are now endangered. Many people are trying to save these great apes.
pages.brief: Gorillas stand in a forest where trees have been cut down, and hunters are a danger to them. The great apes are endangered. Nearby, people work to save the gorillas and their forest home, trying to protect them.
